purpose: Feasibility triage of the 43 problems erdosproblems.com marks decidable/falsifiable/verifiable. Upstream classifies decidability IN PRINCIPLE; this file classifies reachability IN PRACTICE. The default verdict is WALL and most entries earn it: the tag is applied precisely when a conjecture is BELIEVED TRUE, so the finite object it advertises is the one nobody expects to exist. Read this as a screening result, not a target list.
criteria: the finite object is concrete — you can say exactly what a witness is
the search space at the smallest untested case is reachable on one workstation
verifying a candidate is cheap and EXACT — no floats, no CAS
nobody with better tools has already swept it

entries.upstream_handle: VERIFIABLE (open, but could be proved with a finite example) -- $25 from Erdos for a non-existence proof, $2000 from Selfridge for an explicit example
entries.statement_short: Is there a distinct covering system all of whose moduli are odd? A covering system is a finite set of congruences a_i mod n_i, all n_i distinct and > 1, such that every integer satisfies at least one. Asked by Erdos and Selfridge (sometimes with Schinzel).
entries.what_a_witness_is: NOT CONCRETE IN PRACTICE. Nominally a finite list of pairs (a_i, n_i) with distinct odd n_i > 1 covering Z. But nothing bounds the list length or the moduli, and every structurally comparable object we know of is astronomical: our own atlas boards #2/#27 record that a distinct covering system with minimum modulus 40-42 (Nielsen 2009, Owens 2014) already carries more than 10^50 congruences with an lcm period beyond enumeration. A witness is a recursively-defined construction, not a data file.
entries.smallest_untested_case: There is no size parameter to increment -- no 'n' to be at. The live constraints only narrow the shape: an odd covering must use a modulus divisible by 3 (Hough-Nielsen 2019: every distinct covering has a modulus divisible by 2 or 3), its lcm must be divisible by 9 or 15, and it cannot be squarefree (both Balister-Bollobas-Morris-Sahasrabudhe-Tiba 2022, killing the stronger Erdos-Selfridge question outright). Selfridge's reduction (via [Sc67]) to an antichain-moduli covering is dead: no such system exists (see #586).
entries.known_computational_frontier: There is no published exhaustive search frontier to beat -- this is the point. The advances are all theorems: Guo-Sun 2005 (an odd squarefree covering would need at least 22 distinct primes; now moot), Hough-Nielsen 2019 (Ann. of Math., every distinct covering has a modulus divisible by 2 or 3), BBMST 2022 'Covering systems with odd moduli' (Discrete Math., simpler proof plus the 9-or-15 lcm condition, and the full squarefree case). Selfridge's $2000 for an explicit example has stood unclaimed since the 1970s; Filaseta-Ford-Konyagin report Erdos was convinced an odd covering DOES exist and Selfridge that it does not.
entries.search_space_estimate: UNKNOWN, and honestly so. Density is not the obstruction -- sum of 1/n over odd 3 <= n <= 15 is already 1.0218 > 1 -- the obstruction is structural, and no argument bounds where a witness could live. The one hard number available is the cost of CHECKING: covering Z means covering all residues mod L = lcm(n_i), and for witnesses of the known comparable shape L is astronomically large, so there is no flat enumerate-a-period verifier.
entries.verdict_reason: AGREEING with our existing atlas classification, and the prior wall still looks right -- if anything it is understated. This fails criterion 3, not just criterion 2: verification of a realistic candidate is NOT a cheap exact finite check, because you would have to cover every residue class mod an lcm far past enumeration, so confirmation requires structured CRT/inclusion-exclusion reasoning over a recursively-defined object rather than a byte-capped witness check. That is exactly the 'witness not representable' wall reason already recorded on our covering-system boards #2 and #27 ('a min-modulus-40+ covering system already has > 10^50 recursively-defined congruences; no flat poly-time check'), and it transfers verbatim. Add: there is no computational frontier to beat (every advance since 1967 is a theorem), no size parameter to increment, and the search cannot be SAT/ILP-encoded at witness scale. Keep as WALL.

entries.upstream_handle: DECIDABLE ("Resolved up to a finite check"), $500 prize
entries.statement_short: Erdos-Faber-Lovasz: if G is an edge-disjoint union of n copies of K_n, is chi(G)=n? Equivalently, is every linear hypergraph on n vertices n-edge-colourable?
entries.what_a_witness_is: CONCRETE: a linear hypergraph H on n vertices (equivalently a partial linear space / a set of n cliques K_n pairwise sharing at most one vertex) whose chromatic index exceeds n. Refuting n-colourability is a coNP claim, but at these sizes it is a SAT UNSAT call with a checkable DRAT proof.
entries.smallest_untested_case: n = 13 hyperedges-count m = 33 (i.e. linear hypergraphs on 13 vertices with m in [33,54] — the exact band Kirchweger-Peitl-Szeider could not close).
entries.known_computational_frontier: Hindman 1981 [Hi81]: all hypergraphs with at most 10 vertices (in fact whenever the >=3-element edges span <=10 vertices). Romero & Alonso-Pecina 2014, Discrete Math. Algorithms Appl. 6(3):1450039, title literally "The Erdos-Faber-Lovasz conjecture is true for n <= 12", built on Betten & Betten's enumeration of linear spaces on <=12 points. Kirchweger, Peitl, Szeider, SAT 2023 (LIPIcs vol 271, paper 13) re-verified n<=12 with DRAT proofs and extended in bands: Theorem 14 gives n=13, m in [13,32] u [55,78]; n=14, m in [14,28] u [70,91]; n=15, m in [15,29] u [84,105]; n=16, m in [16,30] u {99} u [101,120]; n=17, m in [17,30] u [117,136]; n=18, m in [18,31] u [134,153]. Their longest terminating case (n=15, m=85) took 2d15h; everything else hit a 3-CPU-day cutoff. NOTE: the erdosproblems.com remarks are stale here — they cite only Hindman and do not mention the 2014 or 2023 work.
entries.search_space_estimate: n=13, m=33: candidate line-sets are 33-subsets of the 2^13-1-13-C(13,2)=8100 subsets of [13] of size >=3, so <= C(8100,33) ~ 10^92 before linearity and isomorphism pruning; the SMS pipeline that fully cleared n<=12 timed out at >3 CPU-days on exactly this band.
entries.verdict_reason: Our existing WALL judgement STANDS, and for a sharper reason than we had. Two independent kills. (1) The top of the finite check is not finite in any usable sense: KKKMO21's proof covers only "sufficiently large n" via absorption/nibble with no explicit threshold, so even a complete sweep of n=13 leaves n=14..N_0 with N_0 unknown — the DECIDABLE tag is nominal. (2) The bottom is already at a hard SAT wall: the state of the art (SMS co-certificate learning, 2023) closed n<=12 and then failed on the middle-m band at n=13 after 3 CPU-days per case. We would be re-entering exactly where a purpose-built symmetry-modulo SAT framework stopped, with no new idea. Worth logging separately: our atlas (and upstream's remarks) should be corrected from "Hindman, n<10" to "n<=12 complete, banded to n<=18".

entries.upstream_handle: FALSIFIABLE ("Open, but could be disproved with a finite counterexample")
entries.statement_short: Can every triangle-free graph on 5n vertices be made bipartite by deleting at most n^2 edges? (Erdos' n^2/25 max-cut conjecture.)
entries.what_a_witness_is: CONCRETE as an object: a triangle-free graph G on 5n vertices whose bipartization number (edges minus max-cut) exceeds n^2. But the object is only half a witness — certifying it requires proving max-cut(G) < e(G) - n^2, i.e. an exact max-cut upper bound on a 5n-vertex graph, which is NP-hard and at n>=41 (205 vertices) not tractable exactly.
entries.smallest_untested_case: 5n = 205 vertices (k=41), given Ferudun's claim that a(5k)=k^2 for k<=40. Discounting that claim, the smallest multiple of 5 not settled by exhaustive computation is 5n = 25 vertices (McKay's exhaustive frontier is n=23 vertices).
entries.known_computational_frontier: OEIS A389646 ("Maximum number of edges that need to be removed from a triangle-free graph on n vertices to make it bipartite", Beregovsky, Oct 2025) is exact for n=1..23, a(23)=20 contributed by Brendan McKay, Oct 2025, via maximal triangle-free graphs (House of Graphs / McKay's extremal-graph data) — not full enumeration. Alper Ferudun, arXiv:2606.28041 (Jun 2026), Theorem 1.1, claims a(5k)=k^2 for all 1<=k<=40, i.e. the conjecture verified for 5n = 25,30,...,200 by a per-root-MaxCut-envelope + blow-up-integrality argument, not by search. Best general bound: Balogh, Clemen, Lidicky (arXiv:2103.14179), a(n) <= n^2/23.5. Also a(n) <= a(n-1) + n/5 (Martin Fuller, via Andrasfai-Erdos-Sos). Background enumeration limit: A006785 (triangle-free graphs) is known only to n=17 (3.17x10^13).
entries.search_space_estimate: The number of triangle-free graphs on n vertices is 2^(n^2/4 + o(n^2)). At n=205: 2^10506 ~ 10^3163. Even discounting Ferudun and taking n=25: 2^156 ~ 10^47 — already ~30 orders of magnitude past the n=17 enumeration frontier.
entries.verdict_reason: Robustly a wall under both readings of the literature, which is the useful part. Take Ferudun's June 2026 result at face value and the smallest open case sits at 205 vertices, where the candidate space is 10^3163 and exact max-cut certification is hopeless. Discount it entirely (we should — our own vetting pattern this month was 5 of 6 external claims with sound math and broken verification) and the smallest open case is 25 vertices, still 10^47 graphs against an enumeration frontier of 17 vertices reached by McKay. Separately, condition 3 fails outright: a candidate counterexample cannot be cheaply certified, because proving the deletion number is large is an exact max-cut *upper* bound, i.e. coNP-hard, on a graph far too big for exact solvers. Two of the four conditions fail independently. Not worth a probe.

entries.upstream_handle: FALSIFIABLE — "Open, but could be disproved with a finite counterexample." ($1000 prize; erdosproblems.com/64, last edited 10 Apr 2026)
entries.statement_short: Erdős–Gyárfás: does every finite graph with minimum degree >= 3 contain a cycle of length 2^k for some k >= 2 (i.e. length 4, 8, 16, 32, ...)? Liu–Montgomery [LiMo20] settled it for minimum degree above some absolute constant, so the live case is small minimum degree, essentially delta = 3.
entries.what_a_witness_is: CONCRETE. A finite simple graph G with delta(G) >= 3 whose cycle-length set omits every power of two >= 4. Delivered as an adjacency matrix / graph6 string. The tractable sub-case: a CUBIC graph on 30 vertices with no C4, no C8, no C16 (32 > 30, so only three forbidden lengths). Markström's own reduction (Congr. Numer. 171 (2004)) shows a minimal counterexample has its degree->=4 vertices forming an independent set, and arXiv:2605.22844 (2026) strengthens this to ">= 4/7 of the vertices have degree exactly 3" — both point the search at the cubic lane.
entries.smallest_untested_case: Cubic graphs on n = 30 vertices. Markström generated ALL cubic graphs on fewer than 29 vertices (so <= 28; cubic orders are even, hence 30 is literally the next case). Separately, the non-cubic lane's smallest untested case is n = 16: Royle generated all C4-free graphs with the forced degree structure on fewer than 16 vertices.
entries.known_computational_frontier: Klas Markström, "Extremal graphs for some problems on cycles in graphs", Congr. Numer. 171 (2004) — primary source read at abel.math.umu.se/~klasm/Uppsatser/cycex.pdf, Section 4. Verbatim: he used Brinkmann's generator minibaum "to generate all cubic graphs on less than 29 vertices" plus a Fortran check for cycles of length 4, 8 and 16; no counterexample. Gordon Royle, using a modified makeg, "generated all relevant graphs on less than 16 vertices" (C4-free, with the independent-high-degree structure); no counterexample. Markström's Table 3 gives the number of cubic graphs with no C4 and no C8: n=24 -> 4, n=26 -> 23, n=28 -> 251. Wikipedia summarises this as "counterexample >= 17 vertices, cubic counterexample >= 30 vertices". I checked for any extension since 2004: arXiv:2605.22844 (2026) and arXiv:2308.05675 both cite only Royle–Markström and add no new computation. The frontier is 22 years old and has not moved.
entries.search_space_estimate: All cubic graphs on 30 vertices = 845,480,228,069 ≈ 8.45e11 (OEIS A002851; the sequence is tabulated out to 32 vertices = 1.89e13, direct evidence the class is generatable). At ~4e6 graphs/sec/core for snarkhunter-class generators that is ~59 core-hours, i.e. ~4 hours on a 16-core box; the C4/C8 filter is an early-abort bounded DFS and the surviving class is tiny (251 at n=28, so ~10^3 at n=30). Total ≈ 1e12 primitive ops, dominated by generation. n = 32 is ~1.9e13 graphs ≈ 3-4 days on the same box.
entries.verdict_reason: All four criteria pass for the cubic sub-lane. (1) Witness is a graph6 string. (2) 8.45e11 generations ≈ 1e12 ops with C4/C8 early-abort — one workstation, days not years. (3) Verification is bounded-DFS cycle detection on integers: dependency-free, exact, no floating point, no CAS. (4) Nobody has swept n=30; the published frontier is Markström 2004 and two independent 2026 papers confirm it is still the state of the art. CORRECTION TO OUR ATLAS: we had #64 filed as a WALL. That wall is right for the FULL conjecture (min degree >= 3, arbitrary degrees, unbounded n — no finite check settles it) but WRONG for the cubic lane, which is a clean records-lane cell. The honest deliverable is two exact integers, not a resolution: "no cubic counterexample on 30 vertices" plus the n=30 (and ideally n=32) entries of Markström's Table 3 — extending a 22-year-old published table by one or two rows, verifiable by a stranger from the graph6 output. It does NOT settle the conjecture and must not be described as doing so.

entries.upstream_handle: https://www.erdosproblems.com/97
entries.statement_short: Does every convex polygon have a vertex with no other 4 vertices equidistant from it? ($100, tagged FALSIFIABLE. Erdos's route to #96.)
entries.what_a_witness_is: A convex polygon on n vertices (n points in convex position in R^2) such that EVERY vertex v has at least 4 other vertices lying on a common circle centred at v. Concrete as an object; but the coordinates are real, and nothing forces them rational or even algebraic of low degree. The Lean spec (FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/97.lean) pins it as ConvexIndep A with HasNEquidistantProperty 4 A over Finset R^2 -- note it quantifies over ALL finite A, with no bound on |A|.
entries.smallest_untested_case: There is none in the usable sense: n is unbounded and the conjecture has no smallest open instance. The state of the art is on the k=3 (not k=4) rung -- Danzer built a convex 9-gon with 3 equidistant vertices per vertex (distance varying by vertex), and Fishburn-Reeds [FiRe92] a convex 20-gon with 3 equidistant per vertex at a COMMON distance, and proved 20 is minimal for their cut variant. For k=4 nobody has published even a candidate n to aim at.
entries.known_computational_frontier: Danzer, 9-point convex polygon, k=3, construction reported in Erdos [Er87b]. Fishburn and Reeds, 'Unit distances between vertices of a convex polygon', Comput. Geom. 1992: convex 20-gon with k=3 at a uniform distance, and 20 proven minimal for the two-part-cut version (formalised as erdos_97.variants.three_unit_distance_cut_min in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures). No published exhaustive or heuristic search for k=4 at any n. The erdosproblems page (last edited 27 Oct 2025) reports no computational work at all.
entries.search_space_estimate: Fixing n and enumerating the combinatorial type first: each of n vertices picks which 4 of the other n-1 are equidistant from it, so C(n-1,4)^n types; at n=20 (the Fishburn-Reeds scale for k=3) that is 3876^20 ~ 10^71.6 -- and each surviving type is then a real-algebraic feasibility problem with 3n = 60 equations in 2n-4 = 36 similarity-reduced unknowns.
entries.verdict_reason: Fails criteria 2, 3 and (fatally) the premise of 4. The falsification target is a point in a semialgebraic set, not a member of a finite list: there is no n to search at, because a counterexample may have any number of vertices and failing at n<=30 proves nothing. Even after fixing n the combinatorial layer alone is ~10^71 at n=20 and each leaf needs a polynomial-system solve, i.e. a CAS. Verification is only exact if a witness happens to have rational or low-degree algebraic coordinates, which nothing guarantees -- the constraint system is overdetermined (3n equations, 2n-4 degrees of freedom), so known witnesses at k=3 exist only through imposed symmetry, and hunting symmetric families is a mathematician's job, not a sweep. Upstream's FALSIFIABLE tag here means 'if false there is a finite object', not 'the finite object is small or locatable'.

entries.upstream_handle: https://www.erdosproblems.com/106
entries.statement_short: Pack n squares with disjoint interiors into the unit square; f(n) = max total side length. Is f(k^2+1) = k? (Tagged FALSIFIABLE. Equivalent, by Praton [Pr08], to the full Erdos-Soifer / Campbell-Staton table f(k^2+2c+1)=k+c/k.)
entries.what_a_witness_is: A refutation is fully concrete and small: 10 squares (for k=3) given as centre, side, rotation angle -- equivalently 10 rational-coordinate quadrilaterals -- that pairwise have disjoint interiors, all sit inside the unit square, and have side-lengths summing to strictly more than 3. Because both the disjointness and the excess are STRICT, any genuine counterexample can be rationalised without loss, so a witness can always be presented in exact rational arithmetic.
entries.smallest_untested_case: k = 3, i.e. n = 10: is f(10) = 3? Exactly known values are only f(k^2)=k for all k (Cauchy-Schwarz, trivial), f(2)=1 (Erdos, k=1) and f(5)=2 (Newman, personal communication to Erdos, k=2). So k=1 and k=2 are settled and k=3 is the first open rung. OEIS A391490 (Terence Tao, Dec 2025) tabulates the CONJECTURED values k+a/k, not computed ones -- do not mistake its b-file for a frontier.
entries.known_computational_frontier: There is essentially none, which is the notable fact here. Baek, Koizumi and Ueoro, arXiv:2411.07274 (Nov 2024), proved the AXIS-PARALLEL variant outright: g(k^2+2c+1) = k+c/k for all -k<c<k, which determines g completely -- so every remaining degree of freedom in f is tilt. Raj Singh, arXiv:2601.22163 (Jan 2026), added only an equivalence (the conjecture for all k <=> for infinitely many k <=> convergence of sum_k (f(k^2+1)-k)); explicitly no numerics. Halasz [Ha84] gives the general lower-bound constructions. No published numerical or global-optimisation sweep of f(10) with tilted squares was found. Jineon Baek (a co-author of the axis-parallel result) is listed on the problem page as actively working on it and has flagged it 'difficult'.
entries.search_space_estimate: Not an enumeration: 10 squares x 4 continuous parameters (x, y, side, angle) = 40-dimensional constrained global optimisation, minus 1 for the unit-square symmetry group's discrete action. Cost of a multistart attack is bounded by choice, not by the problem -- ~10^6 restarts x ~10^3 SLSQP iterations x ~45 pair constraints ~ 5x10^10 primitive ops, comfortably one workstation. Exhaustive certification: UNKNOWN (no finite contact-graph enumeration is known for tilted square packings).
entries.verdict_reason: The only one of the four where criteria 1 and 3 are cleanly met and the case is genuinely tiny. A refutation of the ENTIRE Erdos-Soifer table reduces (via Praton) to ten squares in a unit square, and a candidate is checked exactly in rationals by separating-axis tests on 45 pairs plus a rational sum -- dependency-free, milliseconds, no floating point, no CAS. That is a real verifier we could ship. What holds it back from TARGET is criterion 2 in its honest form: the space is continuous, so the search is heuristic and CANNOT certify the negative. Success requires a 90-year-old conjecture to be false at its very smallest untested instance, immediately after its axis-parallel shadow was proved true -- low prior. Concrete recommendation: build the exact rational verifier and run a bounded multistart sweep of n=10 as a cheap, time-boxed refutation attempt; do NOT plan a publishable result on the assumption it finds something, and do not report a numerically-optimal f(10)=3.000 as a computed value -- it would be an uncertified restatement of the conjecture.

entries.upstream_handle: https://www.erdosproblems.com/107
entries.statement_short: Happy Ending problem. f(n) = least N such that any N points in general position contain a convex n-gon. Prove f(n) = 2^(n-2)+1. ($500 for a proof, $100 for a disproof; Graham offers $1000. Tagged FALSIFIABLE.)
entries.what_a_witness_is: A refutation is concrete and cheaply checkable: a set of 2^(n-2)+1 points in R^2, no three collinear, containing NO convex n-gon. For the first open case n=7 that is 33 rational points with no convex 7-gon. (A proof, the $500 direction, is not a finite object at all -- it is a statement for all n.)
entries.smallest_untested_case: n = 7, i.e. does some 33-point set in general position avoid a convex 7-gon? Settled below that: f(4)=5 (Klein 1931), f(5)=9 (Turan and Makai), f(6)=17 (Szekeres and Peters 2006, exhaustive computer search). f(n) is unknown for every n >= 7.
entries.known_computational_frontier: f(6)=17 by Szekeres-Peters (2006) at ~1500 CPU-hours over order types; re-proved by SAT in a few CPU-hours, then 10 CPU-minutes by Scheucher (2023), then 8.53 CPU-SECONDS by Heule and Scheucher (2024). The same group's machinery settled the empty-hexagon problem at 30 points (arXiv:2403.00737). For n=7 the state of the art is arXiv:2512.24061, 'Notes on the 33-point Erdos-Szekeres problem': a triple-orientation SAT encoding with 4-set convexity constraints and convex-layer anchoring, which produces UNSAT certificates only for a COLLECTION OF ANCHORED SUBFAMILIES, and reports heavy-tailed runtime variance as the dominant obstacle. The full 33-point case is open. Lower bound 33 stands from the Erdos-Szekeres 1960 construction; best upper bound is 2^(n+O(sqrt(n log n))) (Holmsen-Mojarrad-Pach-Tardos 2020).
entries.search_space_estimate: Order types of 33 points: the count is 2^Theta(n log n), roughly n^(4n) = 33^132 ~ 10^200; exact enumeration exists only up to n=11 (2,343,203,071 order types, Aichholzer). The SAT reformulation has C(33,3) = 5456 orientation variables, i.e. 2^5456 raw assignments before axioms, and per arXiv:2512.24061 the realistic instances are heavy-tailed even after anchoring.
entries.verdict_reason: Confirms our existing atlas wall -- the judgement still looks right, and for a sharper reason than 'it is hard'. Note the asymmetry we should record: VERIFYING a hypothetical counterexample is trivial (C(33,7) = 4,272,048 subsets, each an exact rational convex-position test -- seconds), so criteria 1 and 3 pass. It dies on 2 and 4. Criterion 2: the search space is ~10^200 order types and the SAT encoding is heavy-tailed at 33 points. Criterion 4 is the decisive one -- this is the most heavily-swept problem in the four: Heule and Scheucher, who hold the world record on exactly this encoding family (ES(6) in 8.53 CPU-seconds, empty hexagon at 30 points), plus a dedicated 2025 preprint, are actively grinding the 33-point case and have covered only anchored subfamilies. Entering that lane means competing with the best SAT-for-discrete-geometry group alive on their own encoding. No lane for us.

entries.upstream_handle: FALSIFIABLE — "Open, but could be disproved with a finite counterexample"; carries a $250 Erdos prize (erdosproblems.com/114, last edited 23 Jan 2026). Previously classified WALL in our atlas.
entries.statement_short: For monic p in C[z] of degree n, is the length of the lemniscate {z : |p(z)|=1} maximised by p(z) = z^n - 1? Not formalised (Lean file absent — 404 in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures).
entries.what_a_witness_is: Semi-concrete: a single monic polynomial of degree n whose lemniscate is LONGER than that of z^n-1. Finitely many complex coefficients — but the discriminating quantity is an arc length, a transcendental integral, not a combinatorial count.
entries.smallest_untested_case: n = 3. Eremenko-Hayman [ErHa99] proved the full conjecture for n=2; Tao [Ta25] (arXiv:2512.12455v2, Dec 2025, 56 pp.) proved z^n-1 is the unique maximiser up to rotation/translation for all SUFFICIENTLY LARGE n. Crucially, the abstract states no explicit threshold n_0, so the residual window is not even a known finite range of n — the same ineffective-n_0 pattern we already logged on Sendov.
entries.known_computational_frontier: Purely analytic, no computational sweep reported anywhere. Dolzhenko [Do61] f(n) <= 4*pi*n; Pommerenke [Po61] f(n) << n^2; Borwein [Bo95] f(n) << n; Eremenko-Hayman [ErHa99] f(n) <= 9.173n and n=2 exactly; Danchenko [Da07] f(n) <= 2*pi*n; Fryntov-Nazarov [FrNa09] proved z^n-1 is a LOCAL maximiser and f(n) <= 2n + O(n^{7/8}); Tao [Ta25] all sufficiently large n. Nobody has published a numerical search over coefficient space, which is itself telling.
entries.search_space_estimate: n=3: monic cubic modulo translation (kill the z^2 term) and rotation gives p(z)=z^3+az+b with a,b in C and one residual real symmetry — about 3 free real parameters, and the region is NON-compact. Small in dimension, but the objective at each point is a certified arc length of an implicit algebraic curve, so there is no primitive-operation count to quote: UNKNOWN as a discrete search, because it is not a discrete search.
entries.verdict_reason: The existing atlas wall is CORRECT and got stronger since it was set. Fails criterion 3 outright: confirming a candidate means computing the length of {|p|=1} to certified precision, i.e. rigorous numerical integration with interval arithmetic on an implicit curve — the exact floating-point dependency we refuse to ship. Fails criterion 2 in spirit: the space is a non-compact 3-real-parameter continuum at n=3 and a 2n-parameter one in general, and Fryntov-Nazarov already proved z^n-1 is a local maximiser, so any counterexample is a distant competing local max that local search will not stumble onto. And the payoff is nil: Tao closed all large n in Dec 2025 with an unstated n_0, so even a clean rigorous n=3 verification settles one value out of an unbounded residual window and yields no headline. The $250 prize is a lure, not a signal of tractability.

entries.upstream_handle: FALSIFIABLE — "Open, but could be disproved with a finite counterexample." ($250 prize; erdosproblems.com/128, last edited 31 Oct 2025)
entries.statement_short: Erdős–Rousseau: if G on n vertices has the property that every induced subgraph on >= floor(n/2) vertices spans more than n^2/50 edges, must G contain a triangle? Equivalently (Razborov's phrasing): every triangle-free n-vertex graph has an induced subgraph on n/2 vertices with at most n^2/50 edges.
entries.what_a_witness_is: CONCRETE but expensive to certify. A triangle-free graph G on n vertices such that min over all S with |S| = floor(n/2) of e(G[S]) is strictly greater than n^2/50. The witness is an adjacency matrix; the certificate that it IS a witness requires a proven MINIMUM over all half-subsets.
entries.smallest_untested_case: There is no meaningful smallest case: the problem's content is asymptotic. The extremal families meet the bound EXACTLY at every n, not just in the limit. For C5[t] on n = 5t vertices, taking two non-adjacent classes whole (2t vertices) plus t/2 vertices from a class adjacent to exactly one of them costs (t/2)*t = t^2/2 = n^2/50 edges — exactly the threshold, and the hypothesis demands strictly more. So the whole small-n regime is pinned to the bound and no perturbation of a blow-up can win. The first n at which an exhaustive triangle-free sweep leaves reach is about n = 15 (1.42e10 graphs).
entries.known_computational_frontier: No exhaustive computational search found in the literature. The frontier is analytic: Erdős–Faudree–Rousseau–Schelp [EFRS94] proved it with 50 replaced by 16; Krivelevich [Kr95] with n/2 replaced by 3n/5 and 50 by 25; Keevash–Sudakov [KeSu06] under e(G) <= n^2/12 or e(G) >= n^2/5; Norin–Yepremyan [NoYe15] for e(G) >= (1/5 - c)n^2; Razborov [Ra22], by flag algebras, proved it with 1/50 replaced by 27/1024 ≈ 0.026367, and proved the full conjecture for girth-5 graphs, graphs of bounded independence number, and strongly regular graphs. The true constant is therefore trapped in [1/50, 27/1024] — a gap of 0.0064.
entries.search_space_estimate: Triangle-free graphs on n vertices (OEIS A006785): n=14 -> 4.68e8, n=15 -> 1.42e10, n=16 -> 5.81e11, n=17 -> 3.17e13. Verifying one candidate costs C(n, floor(n/2)) subset evaluations: C(16,8) = 12,870. A full n=16 sweep = 5.81e11 * 1.29e4 ≈ 7.5e15 primitive ops — about 10^4 times over budget. And the only n small enough to sweep (n <= 14, ≈1.6e12 ops) sit in the regime where n^2/50 < 4 and the C5 blow-ups already sit exactly on the bound.
entries.verdict_reason: PRIOR ATLAS WALL CONFIRMED — and for a stronger reason than headcount. Criterion 2 fails (7.5e15 ops at the first out-of-reach size) and criterion 3 fails: certifying a witness needs the exact MINIMUM number of edges over all floor(n/2)-subsets, which is the minimum-edge-k-subgraph problem — NP-hard, so an exact certificate needs an ILP/branch-and-bound, not a dependency-free checker, for any n past ~34. The killer is structural, not computational: the extremal family hits n^2/50 exactly at every n, so a counterexample must strictly beat a tight family in the regime where Razborov's flag-algebra bound already squeezes the constant to [0.02, 0.02637]. Nothing an enumerable graph can do reaches that.

entries.upstream_handle: FALSIFIABLE — "Open, but could be disproved with a finite counterexample." (no prize listed; erdosproblems.com/167, last edited 13 Oct 2025)
entries.statement_short: Tuza's conjecture: if G has at most k pairwise edge-disjoint triangles, can G be made triangle-free by deleting at most 2k edges? I.e. tau(G) <= 2*nu(G), where nu is the maximum edge-disjoint triangle packing and tau the minimum triangle edge-transversal. K4 and K5 show 2 is best possible.
entries.what_a_witness_is: CONCRETE, with a two-sided certificate. A graph G with tau(G) > 2*nu(G), shipped as an adjacency matrix plus (a) an explicit edge-disjoint triangle packing of size nu together with a proof of maximality, and (b) a proof that no edge set of size 2*nu hits every triangle. Both halves are pure-integer combinatorial optimisations — exact branch-and-bound, no floating point, no CAS. On <= 30 vertices this is seconds per candidate.
entries.smallest_untested_case: n = 9 is the first order that requires any enumeration at all: Puleo proved the conjecture whenever mad(G) < 7, and every graph on <= 7 vertices has mad <= 6, while on 8 vertices only K8 reaches mad = 7 (and K8 has tau = 12 <= 2*nu = 16). The first order where enumeration is nontrivial — and where I could find no published sweep — is n = 11 or n = 12.
entries.known_computational_frontier: No published exhaustive search over general graphs was found. The only exhaustive search located is Puleo (arXiv:1308.2211v3, European J. Combin. 2015, Section 3): a geng run with a custom pruning function for his forbidden configurations, restricted to genus <= 2, which "identified a set of only 5299 graphs that contains any smallest counterexample of genus 2", and he notes "for higher gamma, this computational approach quickly becomes intractible". The frontier is otherwise structural: Puleo shows any minimum counterexample is robust and therefore has minimum degree at least 5, that 6-minus-vertices form an independent set, and that mad < 7 suffices; Botler–Fernandes–Gutiérrez (arXiv:2002.07925) settle treewidth <= 6; Tuza settled planar; Krivelevich settled K3,3-subdivision-free; Haxell [Ha99] gives the general bound (3 - 3/23 + o(1))k; Kahn–Park [KaPa22] settle random graphs; Baron–Kahn settle dense graphs asymptotically.
entries.search_space_estimate: OEIS A000088: 274,668 graphs on 9 vertices, 1.20e7 on 10, 1.02e9 on 11, 1.65e11 on 12. The two cheap structural filters bite hard: minimum degree >= 5, and mad >= 7 forces a very dense chunk (a K8, or a 9-subgraph with >= 32 of 36 edges, or an 11-vertex graph with >= 39 of 55). At n = 11 that plausibly leaves ~1e6-1e7 candidates, each needing an exact integer tau/nu branch-and-bound at ~1-10 ms: ~1e10-1e11 ops, i.e. hours. n = 12 is ~100x worse and sits at the edge.
entries.verdict_reason: The softest of the five, and the only one not previously triaged by us. Criteria 1 and 3 pass cleanly — the witness is a graph and both tau and nu are exact integer optimisations a dependency-free branch-and-bound can settle for small n. Criterion 2 passes at n = 11 and marginally at n = 12 after the min-degree-5 and mad>=7 filters. Criterion 4 is the honest doubt: I found NO published general-graph sweep, but absence of publication on a famous conjecture is weak evidence — a null result at n <= 12 is exactly the kind of thing people run and never write up, so we would risk reproducing folklore. And the deliverable is only a table cell ("no counterexample on <= 12 vertices, certified"), not a resolution: the structural constraints force a counterexample to contain a dense chunk, and dense graphs are precisely where Baron–Kahn already prove the conjecture asymptotically, so a small counterexample is unlikely on priors. Recommend: do a cheap 30-minute reconnaissance at n <= 10 to validate the tau/nu verifier against K4, K5 and Puleo's structural predictions before committing any real compute to n = 11-12.

entries.upstream_handle: FALSIFIABLE — "Open, but could be disproved with a finite counterexample" (erdosproblems.com/242)
entries.statement_short: Erdős–Straus: for every n>2 there exist distinct 1<=x<y<z with 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z.
entries.what_a_witness_is: A single integer n>2 (WLOG prime) together with a certified exhaustive search showing no (x,y,z) works. The witness is really the *exhaustion*, not the number: 'no solution' for one n is itself a nontrivial finite check over divisors of n·x.
entries.smallest_untested_case: n prime, n > 10^18, restricted to n in one of Terzi's 198 bad residue classes mod 120120 (equivalently n = 1,121,169,289,361,529 mod 840 after Mordell). Smallest concrete untested n is the least prime above 10^18 in those classes.
entries.known_computational_frontier: Verified for all n <= 10^18 [MiDu25], cited in the erdosproblems remarks. Prior partial results: Obláth [Ob50] (n+1 divisible by a prime 3 mod 4), Mordell [Mo69] (6 bad classes mod 840), Terzi [Te71] (198 bad classes mod 120120), Vaughan [Va70] exception count <= x·exp(-c(log x)^{2/3}), Elsholtz–Tao [ElTa13] f(p) <= p^{3/5+o(1)}.
entries.search_space_estimate: One decade past the record: pi(10^19)-pi(10^18) ~ 2.05e17 primes x (198/120120 = 0.165% surviving Terzi) ~ 3.4e14 candidate n, each needing its own divisor search over x in (n/4, 3n/4] — >= 3.4e14 heavy checks vs a ~1e12 op budget.
entries.verdict_reason: Frontier is already 10^18 and 100+ years of congruence sieving has removed 99.8% of n, so every remaining case is by construction a hard one. Extending by even one decade needs ~3.4e14 individual exhaustive searches, ~300x over budget before per-case cost. Worse, a positive witness is not a small object: refuting one n requires certifying an exhaustive divisor search, so criterion 3 (cheap exact verification of a witness) fails outright.

entries.upstream_handle: FALSIFIABLE — "Open, but could be disproved with a finite counterexample" (erdosproblems.com/287)
entries.statement_short: If 1 = 1/n_1 + ... + 1/n_k with 1<n_1<...<n_k distinct, must max(n_{i+1}-n_i) >= 3?
entries.what_a_witness_is: Concrete: a finite set S of integers with min a, max b, every consecutive gap <= 2, and sum of reciprocals exactly 1. Equivalently S = [a,b] \ T where T contains no two consecutive integers. Verification is one exact rational sum — trivially cheap and exact.
entries.smallest_untested_case: None below b = 30000. I closed b <= 36 by exhaustive exact DFS over Fractions (0 counterexamples) and refuted every 37 <= b <= 30000 by the p-adic forced-exclusion sieve. Smallest genuinely untested case is max element b = 30001.
entries.known_computational_frontier: No computational bound is recorded anywhere upstream — the remarks cite only Erdős [Er32] (the all-gaps-equal-1 case: 1 is not a sum of reciprocals of consecutive integers) and a conditional reduction to a prime-pair statement. I established the frontier myself this session: no counterexample with max element <= 30000 (scratchpad p287b.py, ~2 min single core).
entries.search_space_estimate: Cost is NOT the obstacle: one linear sieve per candidate top element b, ~b log log b ops, so b <= 1e9 is ~1e10 ops. The exponential fallback (Fibonacci-many independent subsets T, ~1.618^{b-a}) is never reached — it was needed for 0 of the 30000 values of b I scanned.
entries.verdict_reason: Fails criterion 4 for the opposite of the usual reason: the finite search is trivially cheap but empty. For any prime p in [a,b] with floor(b/p)=m small, every multiple of p must be EXCLUDED from S (no nonempty subsum of 1/1..1/m has numerator divisible by p once p > m·lcm(1..m)), yet the excluded set may contain no two consecutive integers. Two forced-adjacent exclusions kill the interval, and that fires for every b in [37, 30000] I tested, with growing slack. This is exactly the page's own remark that a prime p in [N,2N] with (p+1)/2 prime settles it. The residual obstruction is a twin-prime-strength theorem, not compute — no amount of searching produces a witness.

entries.upstream_handle: VERIFIABLE — "Open, but could be proved with a finite example" (erdosproblems.com/307)
entries.statement_short: Are there finite sets of primes P,Q with (sum_{p in P} 1/p)(sum_{q in Q} 1/q) = 1?
entries.what_a_witness_is: Concrete: two disjoint finite lists of primes. Verification is one exact rational multiply — cheap and exact.
entries.smallest_untested_case: Not pinnable. The only hard constraint is |P union Q| >= 60 (from AM-GM: the product being 1 forces sum_{P union Q} 1/p >= 2, and reaching 2 needs the first ~59 primes). No upper bound on the largest prime is known, so there is no well-defined 'next case'.
entries.known_computational_frontier: None recorded. Upstream reports only Cambie's examples for the RELAXED (pairwise-coprime, not prime) version, e.g. 1 = (1+1/5)(1/2+1/3) and 1 = (1+1/41)(1/2+1/3+1/7); and that no example of even the relaxed version is known if 1 is excluded from P and Q. Asked by Barbeau [Ba76]; problem is from [ErGr80].
entries.search_space_estimate: Capping at the first 100 primes (already an unjustified cap — nothing bounds the largest prime) gives 3^100 ~ 5e47 assignments of each prime to P / Q / neither, and any subset must have >= 60 elements. 35 orders of magnitude past budget.
entries.verdict_reason: Passes criteria 1 and 3 (concrete witness, exact cheap check) and fails 2 catastrophically. The search space is not merely large, it is UNBOUNDED — there is no known bound on the largest prime that could appear, so no finite enumeration is ever a complete search. The |P union Q| >= 60 floor guarantees the smallest possible witness already has 60+ primes, so even a bounded heuristic hunt starts at 3^60 ~ 4e28. Nobody has recorded any search at all, which is a signal about tractability, not an opening.

entries.upstream_handle: VERIFIABLE — "Open, but could be proved with a finite example" (erdosproblems.com/364)
entries.statement_short: Are there three consecutive positive integers all powerful (p|n implies p^2|n)?
entries.what_a_witness_is: Concrete: one integer n with the factorizations of n-1, n, n+1. Verification is a handful of exact integer divisions. Structure forces 4|n and n±1 odd powerful, so the witness is equivalently a pair of odd powerful numbers differing by 2 whose midpoint is powerful.
entries.smallest_untested_case: n - 1 > 7.38e28, i.e. the next term of A076445 (pairs of powerful numbers differing by 2) beyond a(13) = 73840550964522899559001927225.
entries.known_computational_frontier: No such n for n < 7.38e28, from OEIS A076445 (Jud McCranie; extended by Reynolds 2005 and T. D. Noe 2006). Noe's parametrization via Sentance [Amer. Math. Monthly 88 (1981) 272-274] and A118894 provably GENERATES ALL consecutive odd powerful pairs from Pell equations x^2-my^2=1, so the enumeration is complete, not heuristic. Max Alekseyev's conjectured table already lists 33 terms, far beyond a(13). Active theory: Chan [Ch25], She [Sh25], arXiv 2503.21485, 2507.16828, 2605.06697; ABC implies only finitely many triples.
entries.search_space_estimate: Naive route: powerful numbers <= X number ~2.173·sqrt(X); at X = 1e29 that is 6.9e14 objects, ~700x over a 1e12 budget just to regenerate the swept range. Pell route: already enumerated by Noe/Alekseyev past the recorded bound.
entries.verdict_reason: Textbook criterion-4 failure. The frontier is 7.38e28 via a PROVABLY COMPLETE Pell-family enumeration (A118894/Sentance), and Alekseyev has 20 further conjectured terms beyond it — the people with the right algorithm have already run it far past where we could. The naive re-enumeration route is 700x over budget. Two 2025 papers are attacking the remaining structured cases theoretically. Nothing for a workstation sweep to add.

entries.upstream_handle: VERIFIABLE — "Open, but could be proved with a finite example" (erdosproblems.com/366)
entries.statement_short: Is there a 2-full n with n+1 3-full? (p|n implies p^2|n; p|n+1 implies p^3|n+1.)
entries.what_a_witness_is: Concrete: one integer n printed with the factorizations of n and n+1. Verification is a few dozen exact integer divisions — no floats, no CAS. Known near-examples in the REVERSE orientation: (8,9) and (12167 = 23^3, 12168 = 2^3·3^2·13^2).
entries.smallest_untested_case: n > 10^22. Concretely: the first cubefull number c in (10^22, 10^24] with c-1 (or c+1, reverse orientation) powerful.
entries.known_computational_frontier: No examples for n < 10^22 — but this bound is INHERITED from OEIS A060355 (consecutive powerful pairs), b-file by Donovan Johnson, 39 terms < 10^22. That is the harder, sqrt(X)-cost search. No sequence or computation exists anywhere for the cubefull-driven version, and OEIS has NO sequence at all for consecutive cubefull pairs (Erdős's weaker question in [Er76d], Guy B16). Page last edited 16 July 2026 and actively curated (Cambie, Stephan, van Doorn), so absence of a deeper bound is meaningful evidence. NOTE: 1 claimed proof is logged on the page — read it first.
entries.search_space_estimate: Only n+1 needs enumerating: #cubefull <= X ~ 4.659*X^(1/3) (constant A362974 = 4.659266..., counts tabulated in A362973; Bateman-Grosswald 1958 / Finch 2003 sec. 2.6.1). Generate as x^5*y^4*z^3 per A036966 (Greathouse), streamed, no storage -- but that stream is NOT deduplicated and emits ~7.65*X^(1/3) = zeta(4/3)*zeta(5/3) raw triples, so budget the raw count, not the distinct one. At X = 1e24: 4.60e8 distinct cubefull, 7.49e8 raw triples, x ~1e3 ops each (trial-divide the neighbour, then a perfect-power test on the cofactor) = ~5e11 ops. X = 1e26 costs 2.14e9 distinct / 3.50e9 raw. MEASURED: our 2026-07-26 sweep to 1e24 emitted exactly 749,400,934 triples in 2.14 core-hours, confirming the raw constant and the ~1e3-ops estimate (certificates/erdos-366/). Our earlier figure '5.5*X^(1/3), A036966' was wrong twice over: A036966 carries no density comment, and 5.5 is 18% high for distinct cubefull numbers and 27% LOW for the raw stream the generator actually emits.
entries.verdict_reason: Only one of the five that clears all four bars. The recorded 10^22 comes from the sqrt(X)-bounded PAIR search; this problem only requires enumerating cubefull numbers, which cost X^(1/3) — so 1e24 fits in ~5e11 ops and 1e26 in ~2.6e12, i.e. 2-4 decades past the record on one workstation with pure integer arithmetic. Caveats, stated up front: (1) the expected outcome is a negative 'verified to N' record, not a resolution — the heuristic count of cubefull c <= X with c±1 powerful scales as X^(-1/6), convergent, and ABC implies finiteness; (2) the upstream statement's orientation contradicts its own worked examples (8 and 12167 are the 3-FULL member, 9 and 12168 the 2-full one), so sweep both orientations — it is free — and flag the discrepancy upstream; (3) the same sweep simultaneously attacks Erdős's weaker consecutive-cubefull question at zero extra cost, and that has never been enumerated at all.

entries.upstream_handle: https://www.erdosproblems.com/375
entries.statement_short: Grimm's conjecture: if n+1,...,n+k are all composite, there exist distinct primes p_1,...,p_k with p_i | n+i.
entries.what_a_witness_is: Concrete. A pair (n,k) such that n+1,...,n+k are all composite and the bipartite graph (interval elements vs. their prime divisors) has NO perfect matching — certified by a Hall-violating subset S of the interval with |union of prime divisors of S| < |S|.
entries.smallest_untested_case: n = 1.9x10^10 + 1 (first n above the Laishram-Shorey verified range). The first record-length composite runs above it: gap 394 after 20,678,048,297; gap 456 after 191,912,783,009.
entries.known_computational_frontier: Laishram & Shorey 2006 (Int. J. Number Theory 2, 207-215) verified Grimm for ALL n <= 1.9x10^10 — ~1 week of Mathematica on a 2.4 GHz Xeon / 2.5 GB, reduced to checking prime indices N <= 8.5x10^8. Theory bounds: Grimm k << log n/loglog n; Erdos-Selfridge k <= (1+o(1))log n; Ramachandra-Shorey-Tijdeman [RST75] k << (log n/loglog n)^3. Nobody has published past 1.9x10^10 in 20 years.
entries.search_space_estimate: Extending 1.9x10^10 -> 2x10^12 = sieve+factor ~2x10^12 integers ~ 10^12-10^13 primitive ops (workstation-weeks). But a Hall violation needs >=2 k-smooth numbers in a length-k composite window sharing a prime pool smaller than their count; at n=10^12 the longest known gap is k<=540 and the expected count of 540-smooth numbers in a 540-window is u^-u with u = log(10^12)/log(540) = 4.4, i.e. ~0.7 — so ~5 of them colliding is astronomically improbable.
entries.verdict_reason: Witness is concrete and verification is exact (trial-division factorisation of <=10^3 integers + Hopcroft-Karp matching, integer-only), but criteria 2 and 4 both fail. Grimm implies p_{n+1}-p_n < p_n^{1/2-c}, i.e. it is STRICTLY HARDER than Legendre's conjecture — a counterexample would require a composite run far longer than Cramer permits. The verified range 1.9x10^10 was reached in 2006 and extending it is linear-cost with essentially zero hit probability. Classic falsifiable-but-unfindable.

entries.upstream_handle: https://www.erdosproblems.com/398
entries.statement_short: Brocard-Ramanujan: are n = 4, 5, 7 the only solutions of n! = x^2 - 1?
entries.what_a_witness_is: Concrete in principle: an integer n > 7 with n!+1 a perfect square (equivalently the pair (n,x)). But at the frontier the object is not writable: n! for n ~ 10^15 has n*log10(n/e) ~ 1.4x10^16 decimal digits (~6 PB).
entries.smallest_untested_case: n = 10^15 + 1. NOTE: the upstream remark ("no other solutions below 10^9, see the OEIS page", page last edited 2026-04-01) is STALE — secondary sources (Wikipedia/HandWiki/Grokipedia, citing Matson and Epstein-Glickman) put the frontier at 10^15. Worth reporting upstream.
entries.known_computational_frontier: Berndt & Galway 2000: n < 10^9. Matson 2017 (unsolvedproblems.org S73, quadratic-residue method): n < 10^12. Epstein & Glickman 2020: n <= 10^15, optimised multi-core C++. Theory: Overholt 1993 — finitely many solutions under weak ABC; Naciri 2025 — finitely many if x±1 is k-free or a prime power, and n=4,5,7 only if x±1 is 7-free.
entries.search_space_estimate: The QR sieve requires primes p > n (for n >= p, n! ≡ 0 mod p and n!+1 ≡ 1 is always a QR — no information), so each prime costs one modular multiply per n: pushing 10^15 -> 10^16 is ~10^16 modmuls per prime and ~50 primes to kill all survivors = ~5x10^17 modular multiplications. Not a one-workstation job by ~3 orders of magnitude.
entries.verdict_reason: Fails criteria 2, 3 and 4. Refuting a candidate is cheap (QR test), but CONFIRMING a witness at n ~ 10^15 requires exact integer arithmetic on a 10^16-digit number — a 6-petabyte object, not a dependency-free certificate. The frontier is already at 10^15 with dedicated multi-core C++, and the heuristic count of solutions beyond n=7 is ~sum 1/sqrt(n!) ~ 0. Only realistic product is a frontier extension nobody can even verify cheaply.

entries.upstream_handle: https://www.erdosproblems.com/458
entries.what_a_witness_is: Concrete and tiny. Reformulation (verified by us): [1..p_{k+1}-1]/[1..p_k] = product of q over all perfect prime powers q^j (j>=2) lying in the gap (p_k, p_{k+1}). So a witness is a single prime gap whose contained prime powers have base-product >= p_k. Since q^2 > p_k forces q > sqrt(p_k), ANY gap containing two prime squares is a counterexample.
entries.smallest_untested_case: p_k > 10^15 (our own run covers everything below). Structurally the first candidate is the first prime gap containing two prime squares — none exists below 10^15.
entries.known_computational_frontier: Upstream remarks give NO computational range (only the two obstructions: ruling out many q with p_k<q^2<p_{k+1}, essentially Legendre; and 'small primes cause trouble'). Our run this session: exhaustive over all 1,962,689 prime powers q^j (j>=2) below 10^15 in 96 s — zero counterexamples; only 5 gaps in all of [1,10^15] contain more than one prime power ((7,11),(23,29),(113,127),(2179,2203),(32749,32771)); max ratio product/p_k = 6/7 = 0.857, attained at the very FIRST case p_k=7. The 'small primes' worry is real but maxes out at 0.857.
entries.search_space_estimate: Cost is one prevprime/nextprime pair per prime power: pi(sqrt(N)) calls. N=10^15 -> 1.96x10^6 calls = 96 s (measured). N=10^18 -> pi(10^9) = 5.08x10^7 calls ~ 1 hour. Witness side: two prime squares in one gap needs p_{k+1}-p_k > (q2-q1)(q2+q1) >= 4 sqrt(p_k), i.e. >4x10^9 at p=10^18, versus the largest known gap below 10^18 of 1476 — short by ~10^6.5.
entries.verdict_reason: The witness hunt is a WALL (needs a prime gap ~10^6 times longer than anything Cramer permits — it is Legendre in disguise). But this is the one entry where the NEGATIVE certificate is genuinely cheap, monotone and unpublished: 'verified for all k with p_k < 10^18' is a dependency-free integer-only frontier statement, ~1 hour of compute, and upstream lists no range at all. Fits our verified-up-to-N records rung exactly. Do NOT fund a witness search; DO consider the 1-hour certificate plus the lcm-ratio reformulation (which makes the check O(pi(sqrt N)) instead of anything involving lcm's).

entries.upstream_handle: https://www.erdosproblems.com/475
entries.statement_short: Graham's conjecture: every finite A subset of F_p\{0} has an ordering a_1,...,a_t whose partial sums are all distinct.
entries.what_a_witness_is: Concrete: a prime p and a set A ⊆ F_p\{0} of size t such that NO ordering has distinct partial sums. Certified by exhaustive backtracking over <= t! orderings (integer arithmetic mod p only).
entries.smallest_untested_case: t = 13 (proved for all t <= 12 by Costa-Pellegrini [CoPe20]; t=13 is the first open size). Since t >= p-3 is also proved, the smallest genuinely open instance is t=13 in F_17: C(16,13) = 560 sets. The first awkward one is t=13 in F_47: C(46,13) = 5.0x10^11 sets.
entries.known_computational_frontier: True for all t <= 12 (Costa-Pellegrini 2020, arXiv 2003.05939; literature also states 'true for subsets of size k<=11 in cyclic groups of prime order'). True for p-3 <= t <= p-1 (Hicks-Ollis-Schmitt). Asymptotic ranges: t <= log p/loglog p [Kr24]; t <= e^{c(log p)^{1/4}} [BeKr24]; t <= e^{c(log p)^{1/3}} [CoDe26]; 1 <<_alpha t <= p^{1-alpha} [PhSa26]; p^{1-c} <= t <= (1-o(1))p [BBKMM25]; t >= (1-o(1))p [MuPo25].
entries.search_space_estimate: A complete sweep of ONE prime is 2^{p-1}/(p-1) sets after the scaling symmetry: p=31 -> 2^30/30 = 3.6x10^7 sets; p=37 -> 2^36/36 = 1.9x10^9; p=41 -> 3.6x10^10. Measured per-set cost (our Python backtracker, t=13, p=17): 4.4 sets/s worst case, i.e. ~0.22 s/set — even a 1000x C speedup leaves p=37 at ~10^5 s. And p is unbounded, so NO sweep ever closes t=13.
entries.verdict_reason: The DECIDABLE label is not backed by a writable number. 'Proved for all sufficiently large p' is assembled from four theorems whose constants are unspecified or ineffective (c in e^{c(log p)^{1/3}}, the <<_alpha in Pham-Sauermann, the o(1) in BBKMM/MuPo), so no explicit p_0 exists and the 'finite check' cannot be enumerated. Exactly the Sendov n_0 = exp(10^126) failure mode we already logged. Meanwhile the small-p end (t<=12, and prime orders up to the literature's computational reach) is already swept, so criteria 2 and 4 both fail. Verification of a candidate counterexample IS cheap and exact — that is the only criterion this passes.

entries.upstream_handle: https://www.erdosproblems.com/488
entries.statement_short: A finite, B = {n>=1 : a|n for some a in A}. Is |B∩[1,m]|/m < 2|B∩[1,n]|/n for every m > n >= max(A)?
entries.what_a_witness_is: Concrete and small: a triple (A, n, m) with m > n >= max(A) violating the inequality. Verified by inclusion-exclusion over subsets of A using floor(x/lcm(S)) — exact integer arithmetic, no floats needed (compare cross-multiplied integers).
entries.smallest_untested_case: No size ladder exists, which is itself the problem. Our sweep this session: ALL A ⊆ [1,14] with |A| <= 4 (1,470 sets, x <= 4000) plus 74,041 random A with |A| <= 8 and max(A) <= 120 (x <= 8000). Max ratio found: 1.991667 at the singleton A={120}, m=240 (n=239). Best non-singleton: 1.849 at A={13,14}. Zero counterexamples.
entries.known_computational_frontier: No published sweep for THIS version. The counterexamples that exist (Cambie's A = primes <= n with m=2n; the concrete ones by Alexeev and Aristotle; the widely-reported Nov-2025 'AI disproved Erdos 488') are all against the [Er61] variant with a∤n instead of a|n, which is believed a typo — upstream restated the problem afterwards. That lane is already harvested. Two contributors (will0708, wesleyaweaverjr) are listed as currently working on the live version, 30 comments.
entries.search_space_estimate: An exhaustive sweep of all A ⊆ [1,24] is 2^24 = 1.7x10^7 sets x an ~8000-term sieve = 1.3x10^11 ops ~ 1 workstation-day. But the extremal family is A={a}, n=2a-1, m=2a giving ratio (2a-1)/a -> 2 as a -> infinity — i.e. the reachable sweep direction (small max(A)) is precisely where the ratio is SMALLEST.
entries.verdict_reason: Passes criteria 1 and 3 cleanly, fails 2 and 4. The constant 2 is best possible and is approached only from below, only by singletons; every multi-element set we measured is strictly worse (<=1.85 vs 1.99), so a bounded sweep is orthogonal to the extremal direction and its negative result would be unpublishable ('no counterexample with max(A)<=24' says nothing about a->infinity). The finite-counterexample lane on this problem number has already been harvested against the mis-stated variant, and two upstream contributors are actively on the live one. Cheap to poke at, but no credible witness direction.

entries.upstream_handle: https://www.erdosproblems.com/506
entries.statement_short: What is the minimum number of distinct circles determined by n points in R^2, not all on a circle (and not all on a line)? Tagged DECIDABLE ('resolved up to a finite check').
entries.what_a_witness_is: Two very different objects, and they must not be conflated. UPPER bound: a concrete n-point rational configuration whose triples fall into few concyclic classes -- exactly checkable (concyclicity of 4 points is a 4x4 determinant = 0 in exact rationals; the circle count is the number of equivalence classes of the C(n,3) triples). LOWER bound / the actual MINIMUM asked for: not a concrete finite object at all -- it is a universally quantified statement over a continuum of configurations at each n.
entries.smallest_untested_case: n = 8 is the first n the remarks explicitly flag as anomalous and unresolved: Segre observed that projecting a cube to the plane beats the naive binom(n-1,2) = 21 bound at n=8, but no exact value of the minimum is stated for n=8 or for any n in the open range. The open range is the whole of roughly 5 <= n <= 393.
entries.known_computational_frontier: Zero, as far as I can find. Elliott [El67] proved at least binom(n-1,2) circles for n > 393; Purdy and Smith found the error and corrected it to binom(n-1,2)+1-floor((n-1)/2) for n > 393, which is best possible (n-1 points on a circle plus one off it); Balint and Balintova [BaBa94] report the same. Segre's cube projection is the only small-n data point on the page. Searches for computed tables of the minimum at small n returned nothing -- the adjacent literature (Lin-Makhul-Mojarrad-Schicho-Swanepoel-Zahl, 'On sets defining few ordinary circles', arXiv:1607.06597) addresses ORDINARY circles, a different quantity, and is itself asymptotic. The erdosproblems page (last edited 01 Feb 2026) says only 'the problem appears to remain open for small n'.
entries.search_space_estimate: At n=8, abstracting to which 4-subsets are concyclic: 2^C(8,4) = 2^70 ~ 1.2x10^21 candidate concyclicity hypergraphs before any realisability filter; pruning to families of maximal concyclic sets pairwise meeting in <= 2 points cuts this a lot but leaves each survivor needing a decision of realisability in the plane, which is an existential-theory-of-the-reals problem requiring real quantifier elimination (a CAS), not arithmetic.
entries.verdict_reason: This is the clearest instance in the batch of the trap the brief warns about: upstream's DECIDABLE tag means 'only finitely many n remain open' (n <= 393), NOT 'a finite check settles each n'. For each individual n the configuration space is a continuum modulo Mobius transformations, so the MINIMUM -- the thing actually asked for -- is not finitely checkable, and confirming a candidate minimum needs realisability decisions that are exists-R and want a CAS, which fails criterion 3 outright. The one genuinely cheap and exact piece is the upper-bound half (rational coordinates + exact 4x4 determinants), and there does appear to be a real gap there -- nobody has published a small-n table, and inversion maps known orchard-problem line configurations to circle configurations, which is a cheap source of candidates. But that is a RECORDS lane producing certified upper bounds, not a resolution of #506, and I do not recommend booking it as progress on the stated problem. If Kevin wants it, frame it honestly as 'certified upper bounds for c(n), 5 <= n <= 20', with the lower-bound column left empty.

entries.upstream_handle: DECIDABLE ("Resolved up to a finite check")
entries.statement_short: If T is a tree on n vertices then R(T,T) <= 2n-2.
entries.what_a_witness_is: CONCRETE: a tree T on n vertices together with a red/blue colouring of the edges of K_{2n-2} containing no monochromatic copy of T. Verification is exact subgraph-containment of a 9-vertex tree in a 16-vertex graph — at most 16!/7! ~ 4.2x10^9 embeddings, seconds with pruning, pure integer arithmetic, no floats, no CAS.
entries.smallest_untested_case: n = 9: the 47 unlabelled trees on 9 vertices (A000055), each tested against K_16 (2n-2 = 16). DS1's exhaustive tables stop at order 8.
entries.known_computational_frontier: Radziszowski, Small Ramsey Numbers DS1 rev. 17 (2024), section 5.4 item (p): "Extensive tables of R(T_m,T_n) for 6 <= m,n <= 8, for many concrete pairs of trees", obtained by adiabatic quantum optimization [RanMCG = arXiv:1606.01078], whose Table 16 covers all 23 trees of order 8. Theory: Zhao [Zh11] proved R(T)<=2n-2 for large n via his resolution of the Loebl-Komlos-Sos conjecture (regularity-based, threshold not explicit); Ajtai-Komlos-Simonovits-Szemeredi announced a full proof for large n, unpublished; Montgomery, Pavez-Signe, Yan (arXiv:2509.07934, 2025) prove Burr's exact formula R(T)=max(2t_1,t_1+2t_2)-1 only for Delta(T) <= cn with c non-explicit. Exact families settled for all n: paths (Gerencser-Gyarfas), stars (Harary), double stars with t_1>=3t_2-2 (Grossman-Harary-Klawe).
entries.search_space_estimate: n=9: 47 trees x 2^C(16,2) = 47 x 2^120 ~ 6x10^37 colourings of K_16 — direct enumeration impossible; the only route is CEGAR/SMS SAT over 120 variables with S_16 symmetry breaking, since a direct encoding needs ~4x10^9 no-mono-T clauses per colour. Number of CEGAR blocking clauses required is UNKNOWN.
entries.verdict_reason: The only one of the five that is not obviously dead, and I am flagging it as MAYBE rather than TARGET deliberately. In its favour: the witness is fully concrete, verification is cheap, exact and dependency-free (tree containment in a 16-vertex graph), the frontier is genuinely at order 9 (DS1 stops at order 8), 47 trees is a small outer loop, and 120 Boolean variables is a size where SMS-style co-certificate learning is the natural and proven tool — the same machinery that cleared EFL n<=12. Against it, honestly: (a) closing n=9 does NOT resolve #547, because Zhao's and AKSS's thresholds are non-explicit, so this is an uncomputed-table-cell result in our records lane, not a problem closure — sell it that way or not at all; (b) the CEGAR iteration count is genuinely UNKNOWN and is the whole risk, since a direct encoding is ~10^9 clauses and I cannot bound the blocking-clause count in one line of arithmetic; (c) I could not confirm whether the unrefereed claim of exhaustive R(T_n,T_m) for n,m<=12 (a Sept 2025 ResearchGate preprint) is real — if it is, n=9 is already swept and this drops to WALL. Recommend a bounded scoping probe: one tree (say the 9-vertex broom, where Burr's bound is tightest), one CEGAR run, hard 6-hour cap, and check the n,m<=12 claim first.

entries.upstream_handle: FALSIFIABLE — "Open, but could be disproved with a finite counterexample." ($100 prize; erdosproblems.com/548, last edited 07 Mar 2026)
entries.statement_short: Erdős–Sós conjecture: for n >= k+1, every graph on n vertices with at least (k-1)n/2 + 1 edges contains every tree on k+1 vertices (equivalently: average degree > k-1 forces every k-edge tree as a subgraph).
entries.what_a_witness_is: CONCRETE. A pair (G, T): a graph G on n vertices with at least (k-1)n/2 + 1 edges, and a tree T on k+1 vertices that is not a subgraph of G. Both are small finite objects and the non-containment is exactly checkable — tree subgraph-isomorphism into an n-vertex host is a 2^k * poly(n) integer DP (colour-coding / Alon-Yuster-Zwick style), no floating point.
entries.smallest_untested_case: Tree side: every tree on <= 7 vertices is already covered, because on 7 vertices every tree is either a spider (at most one branch vertex — two branch vertices at distance >= 2 with diameter 5 needs 8 vertices) or has diameter <= 4, and both classes are settled. So the first uncovered tree is on 8 vertices (7 edges), diameter 5, two branch vertices. Host side: settled whenever the host order exceeds the tree order by at most 4, so the first open cell is host order = tree order + 5, i.e. n = 13 with edge threshold 6*13/2 + 1 = 40 of the 78 possible edges. Crucially this cell is one point of an infinite two-parameter grid: n is unbounded for every fixed tree.
entries.known_computational_frontier: No exhaustive computer search found. Progress is by host order: settled for host order equal to the tree order (Zhou), +1 (Slater–Teo–Yap), +2 (Woźniak), +3 (Tiner), +4 (Yuan–Zhang 2014, arXiv:1403.5430). By tree class: stars (trivial, noted by Erdős himself), paths (Erdős–Gallai), double stars, spiders, and diameter <= 4 (McLennan 2005). Ajtai–Komlós–Simonovits–Szemerédi announced a proof for all sufficiently large k (2008, still unpublished). The site also notes graph-class results: Brandt–Dobson [BrDo96] girth >= 5, Wang–Li–Liu [WLL00] complement girth >= 5, Saclé–Woznik [SaWo97] C4-free, Yi–Li [YiLi04] C4-free complement.
entries.search_space_estimate: First open cell (8-vertex tree, host n = 13, >= 40 edges): OEIS A000088(13) = 5.05e13 graphs on 13 vertices; roughly half sit at or above the median edge count, so ~2.5e13 candidates, times ~1e4 ops for each tree-embedding test ≈ 1e17 primitive ops. Even the min-degree >= ceil(k/2) = 4 and connectedness reductions (a minimal counterexample is connected with min degree > (k-1)/2) do not bring this under 1e14. And a completed cell would only be one point of an infinite grid, since n is unbounded for every fixed tree.
entries.verdict_reason: PRIOR ATLAS WALL CONFIRMED. Criterion 3 passes (tree-containment is exact, integer, dependency-free) and criterion 1 passes, but criterion 2 fails by five orders of magnitude at the first genuinely open cell (~1e17 ops) and — more fundamentally — the search space has no finite bottom. The standard reductions bound the minimum degree of a minimal counterexample below (>= ceil(k/2)) and force connectedness, but nothing bounds n from above for a fixed tree, so "falsifiable" here means only that a counterexample, if it exists, is a finite object; it does not give a finite check. This is exactly the failure mode the triage brief warns about: a real witness that may live arbitrarily far out.

entries.upstream_handle: DECIDABLE ("Resolved up to a finite check")
entries.statement_short: Prove R(C_k,K_n) = (k-1)(n-1)+1 for k >= n >= 3, except n=k=3.
entries.what_a_witness_is: CONCRETE: a graph G on (k-1)(n-1) + 1 vertices containing no C_k and with independence number < n (the matching lower-bound construction, n-1 disjoint K_{k-1}'s, is classical, so only the upper bound can fail). Verification is exact: no independent 8-set is C(64,8) = 4.4x10^9 checks, and C_10-absence is a pruned DFS which terminates fast precisely because the graph must be long-cycle-free.
entries.smallest_untested_case: (k,n) = (10,8): is R(C_10,K_8) = 9*7+1 = 64? The n<=7 rows are fully closed and the n=8 row is closed at k=8, k=9 and k>=34, leaving k in [10,33].
entries.known_computational_frontier: This is a literature frontier, not a search frontier — no one enumerates here. Rows fully settled: n=3,4,5 (classical), n=6 by Schiermeyer 2003, "All cycle-complete graph Ramsey numbers r(C_m,K_6)", J. Graph Theory 44:251-260; n=7 settled, r(C_m,K_7)=6m-5 for m>=7, with r(C_7,K_7)=37 proved independently by Baniabedalruhman-Jaradat and by Cheng et al. Row n=8: r(C_8,K_8)=50 (Jaradat & Alzaleq, SUT J. Math. 43(1), 2007) and r(C_9,K_8)=57 (2011). General upper reach: Bondy-Erdos [BoEr73] k > n^2-2; Nikiforov [Ni05] k >= 4n+2 (= 34 at n=8); Keevash-Long-Skokan [KLS21] k >= C log n / log log n for large n.
entries.search_space_estimate: (k,n)=(10,8): a witness lives among the 2^C(64,2) = 2^2016 ~ 10^607 graphs on 64 vertices; even modulo isomorphism this is ~10^607/64! ~ 10^518.
entries.verdict_reason: Textbook Ramsey wall. The finite object is concrete and cheaply verifiable, and that is the only condition satisfied. The smallest genuinely open cell requires reasoning about graphs on 64 vertices — R(5,5) is unresolved at 43 vertices, so this is well past the world frontier for exhaustive methods, and the space (10^607) is not reachable by any pruning. Note also that every advance in this row for the last twenty years has been a human structural proof of a single cell (r(C_8,K_8), r(C_9,K_8)), never a computation; there is no computational lane here to enter. Compounding it, the DECIDABLE tag is again nominal: KLS21 covers only "large n", so the finite check has no explicit top even if a cell fell.

entries.upstream_handle: DECIDABLE ("Resolved up to a finite check")
entries.statement_short: Show R_3(C_n) <= 4n-3, where R_3(G) is the 3-colour Ramsey number (Bondy-Erdos; intended for n >= 4, since R_3(C_3) = R(3,3,3) = 17 > 9).
entries.what_a_witness_is: CONCRETE: a red/green/blue colouring of the edges of K_{4n-2} with no monochromatic C_n. Verification is exact — for each of the 3 colour classes, a pruned DFS for a cycle of length exactly n on 33 vertices; integer only, no floats.
entries.smallest_untested_case: n = 9: is R_3(C_9) <= 33? OEIS A389335 gives exact values only for n = 3..8 and carries keywords hard,more — a(9) is the first unknown term.
entries.known_computational_frontier: OEIS A389335 (Beregovsky, Oct 2025), R_3(C_n) = r(C_n,C_n,C_n): a(3)=17, a(4)=11, a(5)=17, a(6)=12, a(7)=25, a(8)=16 — and nothing beyond. Note a(5)=17=4*5-3 and a(7)=25=4*7-3 attain the conjectured bound; a(6)=12=2*6 and a(8)=16=2*8 match the even-case value. Theory: Luczak [Lu99] R_3(C_n) <= (4+o(1))n; Kohayakawa-Simonovits-Skokan [KSS05] equality for large odd n; Benevides-Skokan [BeSk09] R_3(C_n)=2n for large even n. Source of record: Radziszowski DS1.
entries.search_space_estimate: n=9: 3^C(33,2) = 3^528 ~ 10^252 colourings of K_33; a direct SAT encoding needs 3 * C(33,9) * 8!/2 = 3 * 38,567,100 * 20,160 ~ 2.3x10^12 no-monochromatic-C_9 clauses.
entries.verdict_reason: Hardest wall of the five. The smallest open case asks for the 3-colour Ramsey behaviour of K_33, and the only classical 3-colour Ramsey number ever determined is R(3,3,3)=17 (1955); R(3,3,4) is still open at [30,31]. So n=9 sits at or past the absolute world frontier for 3-colour Ramsey computation, in a space of 10^252 with a direct encoding two orders of magnitude too large to write down (2.3x10^12 clauses), let alone solve. Cheap verification of a hypothetical witness does not rescue this. And as with #19, #547 and #551, the DECIDABLE tag is nominal: KSS05 and BeSk09 both say "sufficiently large", so there is no explicit upper end to the finite check.

entries.upstream_handle: DECIDABLE — "Resolved up to a finite check." (no prize listed; erdosproblems.com/580, last edited 24 Oct 2025)
entries.statement_short: Erdős–Füredi–Loebl–Sós (the (n/2 - n/2 - n/2) conjecture): if G on n vertices has at least n/2 vertices of degree at least n/2, must G contain every tree on at most n/2 vertices? Zhao [Zh11] proved it for all sufficiently large n, which is why upstream tags it decidable.
entries.what_a_witness_is: CONCRETE. A graph G on n vertices with at least ceil(n/2) vertices of degree at least ceil(n/2), together with a tree T on at most floor(n/2) vertices that is not a subgraph of G. Non-containment is an exact integer subgraph-isomorphism check; there are only A000055 trees to test (106 trees on 10 vertices, 551 on 12), so the per-candidate cost is trivial.
entries.smallest_untested_case: Formally n = 12 (need >= 6 vertices of degree >= 6, test all 6 trees on <= 6 vertices), rising through n = 14, 16, ... — but this is meaningless: the check must run up to Zhao's n0, and n0 is not a number anyone has written down.
entries.known_computational_frontier: None found — no explicit small-n computer verification is reported anywhere I could locate. The "finite check" comes from Yi Zhao, "Proof of the (n/2 - n/2 - n/2) Conjecture for large n", Electron. J. Combin. 18 (2011) #P27. I pulled the paper (math.gsu.edu/yzhao6/n2_Conj.pdf) and read the proof structure directly: Theorem 1.6 states only "There is a threshold n0 such that Conjecture 1.3 holds for all n >= n0" — no numeric value. Section 4 "contains the Regularity Lemma and some properties of regular pairs", and the proof of Theorem 1.6 sets "n0 := max{n1, n2, n3}" where n1, n2, n3 come from regularity-based Proposition 3.1 and Theorem 3.3. So n0 inherits a Szemerédi-Regularity tower-type dependence and is ineffective as written. Prior art: Ajtai–Komlós–Szemerédi [AKS95] proved the (1+eps) asymptotic version, also via regularity.
entries.search_space_estimate: Two independent blowups. (a) The threshold: n0 is regularity-lemma-derived and has no stated numeric value, so the upper end of the "finite" range is unknown and plausibly tower-scale. (b) The per-n cost: OEIS A000088 gives 1.65e11 graphs on 12 vertices, 1.21e13 on 14, and 6.45e23 on 20 — so even if n0 were miraculously as small as 20, the check at that single n alone is 1e23 graphs, eleven orders past a workstation.
entries.verdict_reason: This is the cleanest illustration in the batch of why the upstream state label is not a promise. "DECIDABLE / resolved up to a finite check" is literally true, but the finite check is bounded above by a Szemerédi-Regularity-Lemma n0 that Zhao never makes explicit, and bounded below in cost by the number of graphs on n vertices, which passes 1e23 by n = 20. Criterion 3 is the only one that passes — tree containment is exact and cheap. Criteria 2 and 4 fail catastrophically and criterion 1's witness, while concrete, lives in a space nobody can enumerate. Filing as WALL, with a note for the atlas: #580 is worth carrying as a documented example of an upstream "decidable" tag whose finite handle is ineffective, which is precisely the distinction our feasibility filter exists to make.

entries.upstream_handle: FALSIFIABLE ("Open, but could be disproved with a finite counterexample"). Not formalised — erdosproblems.com/583 reports "Formalised statement? No".
entries.statement_short: Erdős–Gallai path decomposition conjecture: every connected graph on n vertices decomposes into at most ⌈n/2⌉ edge-disjoint paths.
entries.what_a_witness_is: A single connected graph G on n vertices (an adjacency matrix) whose minimum path-decomposition number exceeds ⌈n/2⌉, together with an exhaustive proof that no decomposition into ⌈n/2⌉ paths exists (SAT UNSAT + DRAT, or a finite search tree). Concrete, but note the hard half of the witness is the refutation, not the graph.
entries.smallest_untested_case: n = 7. All connected graphs on n ≤ 6 vertices have Δ ≤ 5 and are therefore covered by Bonamy–Perrett. At n=7 a counterexample must have Δ = 6 (a universal vertex), be non-planar, and not be 3-degenerate — that residual family is only a few hundred graphs. The meaningful sweep target is "all connected graphs on n ≤ 11", with n = 12 the wall.
entries.known_computational_frontier: NO published exhaustive small-n computer sweep found — the entire literature is class-based, not size-based. Classes settled: Lovász [Lo68] (≤ 1 vertex of even degree; also ⌊n/2⌋ paths-and-cycles); Pyber [Py96] (even-degree-induced subgraph a forest); Botler et al., J. Graph Theory 2020 (treewidth ≤ 3); Bonamy–Perrett [BoPe19] (Δ ≤ 5); Blanché–Bonamy–Bonichon [BBB21] (planar); Anto–Basavaraju [AnBa23] (2-degenerate) and Discrete Math. 2024 (3-degenerate); Chu–Fan–Zhou [CFZ26] (even-degree part = K_m, m ≤ 15, n odd). Best unconditional bound: Dean–Kouider [DeKo00] and Yan (1998 thesis), ⌈2n/3⌉ paths — at n=7 that is 5 against the conjectured 4, so the gap being probed is a single path.
entries.search_space_estimate: Connected graphs on n vertices (A001349): n=7: 853; 8: 11,117; 9: 261,080; 10: 11,716,571; 11: 1,006,700,565; 12: 164,059,830,476. A sweep to n ≤ 11 is ~1.0×10^9 graphs; after filtering to Δ ≥ 6, non-planar, non-3-degenerate the survivors are orders of magnitude fewer, and each needs a ~10^3-node path-decomposition search → ≈10^12 primitive ops total. n = 12 at 1.64×10^11 graphs is out of reach on one box.
entries.verdict_reason: Passes the rubric on the letter but the payoff is thin, so I am not calling it a TARGET. In its favour: the witness is concrete, a sweep to n ≤ 11 lands right at the ~10^12 op line, verifying a decomposition is trivial integer work, and I found no published exhaustive small-n verification — so "Gallai's conjecture holds for every connected graph on ≤ 11 vertices" would be a genuine, replayable records-lane fact. Against it, and this is the deciding consideration: the probability of a small counterexample is essentially nil. Δ ≤ 5, planar, 3-degenerate and treewidth ≤ 3 are all already theorems, Dean–Kouider gives ⌈2n/3⌉ unconditionally (only one path above the target at n=7), and sixty years of hand analysis on exactly these small dense cases would have surfaced anything at n ≤ 11. So the honest expected outcome is a null result. Take it only as a cheap records-lane "verified up to N" item with the null clearly pre-registered — never as a route to resolving the conjecture, whose real difficulty (Lovász, Hajós) lives in Eulerian graphs at large n.

entries.upstream_handle: FALSIFIABLE ("Open, but could be disproved with a finite counterexample") — formalised in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures as FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/617.lean, theorem erdos_617, which pins the witness as a function `coloring : Sym2 V → Fin r` on a `V` with `Fintype.card V = r^2+1` admitting no `S` with `S.card = r+1` and some colour `k` absent on all pairs in `S`
entries.statement_short: Erdős–Gyárfás: for r ≥ 3, every r-colouring of the edges of K_{r²+1} contains r+1 vertices whose induced K_{r+1} misses at least one colour (i.e. no "balanced" colouring exists).
entries.what_a_witness_is: A single explicit map from the 325 edges of K_26 to {1,...,5} (a 325-entry integer array) such that every one of the C(26,6)=230,230 six-element vertex subsets sees all 5 colours among its 15 induced edges. Fully concrete, integer-valued, no auxiliary structure.
entries.smallest_untested_case: r = 5, i.e. K_26 with 5 colours. r=3 (K_10) and r=4 (K_17) are proved; r=2 is false. Equivalently: is the complementary/weakened Ramsey number R^5_4(K_6) ≤ 26? The matching lower bound R^5_4(K_6) ≥ 26 already holds because the affine plane of order 5 exists, so a balanced 5-colouring of K_25 is known to exist — the open question is exactly one vertex above a known construction.
entries.known_computational_frontier: r=3 settled by hand: Chung & Liu, "A generalization of Ramsey theory for graphs", Discrete Math. 21 (1978) 117–127, Thm 3.6 gives R^3_2(K_4,K_4,K_4)=10, with the lower bound from their Thm 2.6 product colouring; recorded again as R_{2,3}(K_4)=10 by Harborth & Möller, Discrete Appl. Math. 95 (1999) 279–284. r=4 by Erdős & Gyárfás [ErGy99] (Discrete Math. 1999). The same quantity is studied independently as a "complementary Ramsey number" (Munemasa & Shinohara, arXiv:1406.2050; J. Indones. Math. Soc. 25 (2019) 146–153). Per the erdosproblems.com/617 comment of 15 Jul 2026, r=5 "appears to be open in all of these communities" — no computational attack on r=5 is on record.
entries.search_space_estimate: Naive: 5^325 ≈ 10^227 — hopeless. SAT encoding: C(26,2)=325 edges × 5 colours = 1,625 Boolean variables; constraints = C(26,6)=230,230 six-subsets × 5 colours = 1,151,150 clauses of width 15 ("colour c occurs among these 15 edges") plus 325 exactly-one blocks ≈ 3,900 clauses. Sub-problem that is outright trivial: fix the known affine-plane balanced colouring of K_25 and ask whether it extends by one vertex — 25 variables over 5 values (5^25 ≈ 3×10^17 naive) with 53,130 propagating constraints from the C(25,5) five-subsets, i.e. seconds of SAT time.
entries.verdict_reason: Meets all four criteria and is the strongest of the five. (1) The witness is a 325-integer array — nothing more. (2) The SAT encoding is of sane size (1,625 vars / 1.15M clauses), and there is a genuinely trivial first move: the r=5 boundary sits exactly one vertex above a KNOWN construction (affine plane of order 5 gives a balanced colouring of K_25), so "does the known K_25 colouring extend to K_26?" is a 25-variable CSP solvable in seconds. (3) Checking a candidate is 230,230 × 15 = 3.45M integer lookups — milliseconds, no floats, no CAS. (4) Frontier is r=4 from 1999; r=5 is untouched in three separate literatures.
