Both outcomes are publishable: SAT gives a counterexample witness (falsifying a 27-year-old conjecture), UNSAT gives a DRAT-certified proof of the first new case since 1999. HONEST RISK: the automorphism group is S_26 × S_5 (order ≈ 4.8×10^28), and highly symmetric colouring instances of this shape are exactly where SAT solvers die (cf. our own R(5,5) experience). Mitigation is the standard one — SMS / symmetry-breaking, the same tool Kirchweger–Szeider used to push diameter-2-critical enumeration to n=13. Recommend starting with the K_25-extension sub-problem, which is cheap and settles whether the obvious extremal structure is the obstruction.

entries.upstream_handle: FALSIFIABLE ("Open, but could be disproved with a finite counterexample"). Not formalised — erdosproblems.com/628 reports "Formalised statement? No".
entries.statement_short: Erdős–Lovász Tihany conjecture: if χ(G) = k and G has no K_k, and a,b ≥ 2 with a+b = k+1, then V(G) splits into two disjoint parts of chromatic number ≥ a and ≥ b.
entries.what_a_witness_is: A graph G with ω(G) < χ(G) = 6 that is not (2,5)-splittable. Usefully, non-(2,5)-splittability collapses by monotonicity to a finite local check: for EVERY edge uv, χ(G − u − v) ≤ 4. So the witness is G plus (i) a 6-colouring, (ii) a DRAT/UNSAT certificate that G has no 5-colouring, (iii) an explicit 4-colouring of G − u − v for each of the |E| edges. Concrete — but there is no bound of any kind on |V(G)|.
entries.smallest_untested_case: The pair (a,b) = (2,5), i.e. k = 6: a K_6-free graph with χ = 6 such that deleting the two endpoints of any edge drops χ to ≤ 4. Known pairs are exactly {(2,2),(2,3),(2,4),(3,3),(3,4),(3,5)} (confirmed in the introduction of arXiv:2607.20376), so (2,5) is the smallest open pair, with (4,4) at k=7 next. K_6-free 6-chromatic graphs exist as small as 10 vertices (C5 ∨ C5, ω=4, χ=6) — but that one IS (2,5)-splittable, and there is no theorem bounding where a counterexample could live.
entries.known_computational_frontier: None. There is no computational frontier at all — I found no computer search, no minimum-counterexample-order bound, and no enumeration in the literature. Progress is entirely structural: Brown–Jung [BrJu69] (2,3) and (3,3); Mozhan and Stiebitz independently (2,4); Stiebitz (3,4),(3,5); Balogh–Kostochka–Prince–Stiebitz [BKPS09] (quasi-line graphs, independence number 2); Song, arXiv:1805.11437 (graphs with forbidden holes); Longbrake–Tariq, arXiv:2406.15164 (claw-free, t ≤ 4s−3); Song, arXiv:2607.20376 (all even-hole-free graphs). Comprehensive survey: Song, "The Erdős-Lovász Tihany Conjecture — a survey" (2022).
entries.search_space_estimate: All graphs up to isomorphism (A000088): n=10: 1.2×10^7; n=11: 1.02×10^9; n=12: 1.65×10^11; n=13: 5.0×10^14. So an exhaustive sweep is arithmetically possible only to n ≈ 11 (n=12 already needs ~46 h of χ-computation alone, before generation). Against that: the witness size is UNBOUNDED — no theorem says a minimal counterexample has ≤ 11, ≤ 100, or ≤ 10^6 vertices — so the sweep has no principled stopping point and no reason to contain the object.
entries.verdict_reason: Fails criteria 2 and 3. The killer is that nothing bounds the witness: for a counterexample you need a K_6-free graph with χ = 6, and "high chromatic number without the corresponding clique" is precisely a property that needs room — the constructions that realise it (Mycielski, Kneser, shift graphs) grow fast, and every small χ=6 graph is dense enough that K_6-freeness is nearly self-defeating. A brute sweep to n ≤ 11 is cheap (10^9 graphs) but is searching a region where nobody believes the object lives, so it buys a near-worthless "no counterexample on ≤ 11 vertices" line; beyond n=12 the 2^C(n,2) growth ends it. Verification also fails the cheap-and-exact bar in the honest sense: certifying χ(G) = 6 requires a co-NP lower bound (a DRAT proof that no 5-colouring exists), which is exact and float-free but is a real solver dependency, not the dependency-free checker we ship. Recommend leaving this to the structural community, which is where all sixty years of progress has come from.

entries.upstream_handle: https://www.erdosproblems.com/647 (VERIFIABLE, $44, Erdős–Selfridge; [Er79],[Er79d],[Er92e]; OEIS A087280, A062249)
entries.statement_short: Let τ be the divisor function. Is there some n > 24 with max_{m<n}(m + τ(m)) ≤ n + 2?
entries.what_a_witness_is: A single integer n > 24. Checked by sieving τ(m) for all m < n and confirming the running maximum of m+τ(m) never exceeds n+2. Equivalently τ(n−k) ≤ k+2 for every k ≥ 1, and only k ≲ max τ matters.
entries.smallest_untested_case: n > 6.157×10^17 (= 2520·46189·529·10^7), restricted to n = 2520N with N in one of the 41 open residue classes mod 46189 — everything below that is certified clear.
entries.known_computational_frontier: OEIS A087280 lists 5,8,10,12,24 and 'no more terms < 10^10'. Patrik Idén, segmented multiplicative sieve, exhaustive to 10^12 with no solution, min gap Δ(n)=224 near 10^11 (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.20677388, v2/v3 at 10.5281/zenodo.21084248 and 10.5281/zenodo.21134668, Jun 2026). Scott Hughes, exhaustive search of the 41-residue frontier to n ≈ 6.157×10^17 with a dependency-free laptop-checkable certificate (github.com/scottdhughes/erdos647-proof-chain/tree/main/frontier-certificate, Jun 2026), plus an unconditional density bound |C(x)| ≪ x/(log x)^7 from admissible prime 7-tuples.
entries.search_space_estimate: One further decade = n ∈ (6.16×10^17, 6.16×10^18]; candidates are n=2520N with N in 41/46189 classes, so 6.16×10^18 × (41/46189) / 2520 ≈ 2.2×10^12 candidate n, each needing τ(n−k) for k ≤ 16 on ~10^18-sized integers ⇒ ≳10^13 factoring/primality ops, ≥10× over a one-workstation budget.
entries.verdict_reason: Criteria 1 and 3 pass cleanly, criterion 4 fails hard and 2 fails by ~10×. The frontier moved to 6.16×10^17 in June 2026 with a public, laptop-reproducible certificate — we would be re-treading someone else's two-month-old work at 10× the cost. Worse, the object is receding: the required slack is Δ(n) ≤ 2 and the *minimum* observed slack up to 10^12 is 224, with a fitted growth Δ ≈ 0.069(log m)^2.18 — i.e. the data confirms Erdős's own conjecture that max_{m<n}(τ(m)+m−n) → ∞. The surviving candidates are pinned inside admissible prime 7-tuple families, so existence is Schinzel Hypothesis H territory, not a search question. Do not spend compute here.

entries.upstream_handle: https://www.erdosproblems.com/672 (VERIFIABLE; [Er97c], [Va99,1.32])
entries.statement_short: Can the product of an arithmetic progression n, n+d, …, n+(k−1)d of positive integers with k ≥ 4 and gcd(n,d)=1 be a perfect power?
entries.what_a_witness_is: A tuple (n, d, k, ℓ) with k ≥ 4, gcd(n,d)=1, ℓ ≥ 2 such that ∏_{t<k}(n+td) is an exact ℓ-th power. Verification is a product plus an exact integer ℓ-th root — cheap and exact.
entries.smallest_untested_case: k = 35 with ℓ = 2 or 3 (all ℓ are settled for 4 ≤ k ≤ 34; ℓ = 5 is separately settled for 3 ≤ k ≤ 54). n and d are unrestricted.
entries.known_computational_frontier: There is no computational frontier — the results are theorems, not searches. Euler (k=4, ℓ=2); Obláth [Ob51] for (k,ℓ)=(5,2),(3,3),(3,4),(3,5); Bennett–Bruin–Győry–Hajdu [BBGH06] for 4 ≤ k ≤ 11; Győry–Hajdu–Pintér [GHP09] for 4 ≤ k ≤ 34 and all ℓ; Bennett–Siksek [BeSi20] for all large k with prime ℓ > e^{10^k}; Marszalek [Ma85] gives k ≪_d 1 for fixed d.
entries.search_space_estimate: UNBOUNDED — at k = 35 there is no bound on n or d, so there is no finite region to exhaust. For scale, even a blind sweep of n,d ≤ 10^6 is 10^12 coprime pairs × 35 multiplications on growing integers ≈ 3.5×10^13 ops and covers a measure-zero slice of the space.
entries.verdict_reason: Criterion 2 fails absolutely: 'verifiable' here means only that if an example exists it is a finite tuple, not that it lives anywhere findable. Nothing bounds n or d, and Marszalek's k ≪_d 1 is the wrong direction (it bounds k given d, ineffectively for our purposes). The whole 50-year Baker/modularity line — Erdős–Selfridge, Obláth, BBGH, GHP, Bennett–Siksek — points at non-existence, so a search is hunting an object the theory says is not there in a space with no boundary. This is a Diophantine-theory problem wearing a finite-witness costume.

entries.upstream_handle: https://www.erdosproblems.com/699 (FALSIFIABLE; Erdős–Szekeres [ErSz78], Guy B31)
entries.statement_short: Is it true that for every 1 ≤ i < j ≤ n/2 there exists a prime p ≥ i with p | gcd(C(n,i), C(n,j))?
entries.what_a_witness_is: A triple (n, i, j) with 1 ≤ i < j ≤ n/2 such that no prime p ≥ i divides both C(n,i) and C(n,j). Verified by Kummer's theorem — p | C(n,k) iff adding k and n−k in base p produces a carry — so the check is pure exact integer arithmetic on base-p digits, with no big-integer factoring and no floating point.
entries.smallest_untested_case: n = 10^7 + 1 (general n), outside the special families n = 2^k for k ≤ 27 and n = 3^m + 1 for m ≤ 17, both already covered to ≈1.34×10^8.
entries.known_computational_frontier: Cong Lu, Rust implementation, exhaustive over all (n,i,j) up to n = 10^7 with no counterexample, plus the targeted families above; open-sourced at github.com/conglu1997/erdos_699_rust (comment of 06 Jan 2026 on the #699 thread). The only known counterexample to the stronger 'p > i' variant with i ≥ 4 remains gcd(C(28,5),C(28,14)) = 2^3·3^3·5 [ErSz78]. Theory front is moving fast: GPT-5.6/Price settled j ≤ (3/2)i and n = 2j (accepted proof claim); thread comments of 24–25 Jul 2026 push the settled range to j ≪ i log^2 i unconditionally.
entries.search_space_estimate: A counterexample forces (n−i, n] to be prime-free (any prime there exceeds n/2 and divides both binomials), so i ≤ n − prevprime(n) ≤ 540 for n < 1.8×10^19, and for p > n/2 the test collapses to 'n mod p < k', an interval condition on j. So 10^7 → 10^8 is ≈9×10^7 values of n × ≈18 admissible i on average × ~500 ops ≈ 8×10^11 primitive ops — under the 10^12 budget, and none of the existing search used this pruning.
entries.verdict_reason: The only one of the five that passes all four tests. The witness is a concrete triple; verification is Kummer carry-counting in exact integer arithmetic (our best possible verifier shape); the exhaustive frontier is only n = 10^7, set by one open-source hobby run in Jan 2026; and the prime-gap pruning that collapses the i-range from n/2 to ≤540 was only articulated in the thread on 25 Jul 2026, after that run — so a 100–1000× extension is genuinely available at ~10^11–10^12 ops. Two honest caveats that must go in the board framing, not be discovered later: (a) the conjecture is believed TRUE, so the realistic deliverable is a certified verified-to-N nonexistence record in our records-ladder house style, NOT a counterexample; (b) the lane is crowded — three named workers, an open reference implementation, and a theory front closing j ≪ i log^2 i — so the record has a short shelf life and we should pin the verifier and the certificate format before spending search compute. Note also that one of the July-2026 thread comments is disclosed as written by a Claude Opus 5 agent, i.e. we already have a presence on the theory side of this problem.

entries.upstream_handle: FALSIFIABLE (open, but could be disproved with a finite counterexample)
entries.statement_short: The prime power conjecture [Er81]: if a finite projective plane of order n exists must n be a prime power? A plane of order n is a family of (n+1)-subsets of {1,...,n^2+n+1} such that every pair of points lies in exactly one set.
entries.what_a_witness_is: CONCRETE. A projective plane of order n with n not a prime power. For n=12 that is a 157 x 157 zero-one incidence matrix with exactly 13 ones per row and per column and every point pair on exactly one line -- about 24,649 bits, roughly 3 KB.
entries.smallest_untested_case: n = 12. The conjecture is proved for n <= 11: n=6 by Bruck-Ryser [BrRy49] plus Tarry, n=10 by the Lam-Thiel-Swiercz computer search [La97]; n=14 is also excluded by Bruck-Ryser (14 = 2 mod 4 is not a sum of two squares). So n=12 is the unique open case below 14.
entries.known_computational_frontier: n=10 is the frontier and it was a landmark multi-year effort: Lam-Thiel-Swiercz 1989 consumed thousands of Cray-1 hours plus cluster time, and only in the last few years have pieces of it been independently re-verified with formal UNSAT certificates (Bright et al., arXiv:1911.04032 on weight-15 codewords; arXiv:2001.11974 on ovals). For n=12 only thin slices are excluded: no projective plane of order 12 admits a collineation group of order 8, and none admits one of order 16. The full n=12 case is universally described as far beyond current capability.
entries.search_space_estimate: 157 points, 157 lines of size 13; C(157,13) = 3.39e18 candidates for a SINGLE line, and 157 mutually consistent lines are needed. Even after fixing a pencil and normalising, the residual space dwarfs the n=10 case, whose 111 points and 11-point lines already cost order-1e11 subcase-hours in 1989.
entries.verdict_reason: Criteria 1 and 3 are near-perfect -- the witness is a 3 KB bit matrix and checking it is C(157,2) = 12,246 pair counts, pure integer, sub-millisecond -- which is exactly the trap this triage exists to catch. Criteria 2 and 4 fail catastrophically. The immediately preceding case, n=10, was one of the largest computations in combinatorics history (Lam-Thiel-Swiercz 1989) and is still being re-certified piecewise 35 years later; n=12 is orders of magnitude larger, has resisted every serious attempt, and decades of specialist effort have only shaved off tiny collineation-group slices. Nothing about our machinery gives an edge over the SAT-plus-CAS groups already working the n=10 re-verification. The one honest adjacent lane -- independently re-certifying a slice of the n=10 nonexistence proof -- is someone else's active project, not a frontier we would be extending.

entries.upstream_handle: DECIDABLE ("Resolved up to a finite check") — formalised in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures as FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/742.lean; the file itself carries `variants.fan_bound` (n ≤ 24 or n = 26) and `variants.furedi_bound` (∃ n₀, ∀ n ≥ n₀), which is exactly the shape of the trap here.
entries.statement_short: Murty–Simon conjecture: a diameter-2-critical graph on n vertices (deleting any edge increases the diameter) has at most n²/4 edges, with K_{n/2,n/2} extremal.
entries.what_a_witness_is: A diameter-2-critical graph on n vertices with more than ⌊n²/4⌋ edges — a single adjacency matrix. Verification of a candidate is genuinely trivial (all-pairs distances, then one edge-deletion diameter check per edge: O(n·m) integer work). The witness is concrete and cheap to check; that is not the problem here.
entries.smallest_untested_case: n = 25, then n ≥ 27. Fan, Discrete Math. 67 (1987) 235–240, proved the conjecture for all n ≤ 24 and for n = 26. The "finite check" that the DECIDABLE tag refers to is the whole interval [25, n₀) where n₀ is Füredi's threshold.
entries.known_computational_frontier: Exhaustive enumeration of diameter-2-critical graphs: Radosavljević and Živković computed all of them up to 10 vertices with nauty; Kirchweger and Szeider pushed this to 13 vertices with SMS (SAT modulo symmetries). Theory: Plesník (1975) |E| < 3n(n−1)/8; Fan (1987) n ≤ 24 and n = 26; Haynes–Henning et al. on Murty–Simon I/II; Füredi, "The maximum number of edges in a minimal graph of diameter 2" (1992), proves it for all n ≥ n₀ via the Ruzsa–Szemerédi (regularity) theorem — and that n₀ is a tower of 2's of height about 10^14.
entries.search_space_estimate: Graphs on 25 vertices up to isomorphism ≈ 2^C(25,2)/25! = 2^300/25! ≈ 2.0×10^90 / 1.55×10^25 ≈ 1.3×10^65. The best exhaustive machinery on this exact graph class (SMS) reaches n = 13 — about 12 orders of magnitude short at n=25, and the theoretical gap runs to a tower of 2's of height 10^14, which is not a number that admits arithmetic.
entries.verdict_reason: This is the canonical example of the trap the brief warns about: DECIDABLE here means "resolved up to a finite check" where the finite check is n ≤ tower_2(10^14). Criterion 3 passes beautifully — checking a candidate is O(n·m) integer work — and criterion 1 passes, but 2 and 4 both fail hard, and they fail from opposite directions. From below, the small end is already swept and proved: Fan closed n ≤ 24 and n = 26 by hand in 1987, and Kirchweger–Szeider enumerated the entire class to n = 13, so there is nothing to pick up cheaply. From above, Füredi proved the conjecture outright for large n, so the only place a counterexample could hide is n = 25 or n ≥ 27, where the isomorphism class count is ~10^65 at the very first open value. Extending SMS enumeration from n=13 toward n=25 is a 12-order-of-magnitude ask on a class that is not that restrictive. There is also no headline available even on success: the conjecture is already a theorem for all large n, so closing n=25 would be a footnote, not a result. Note the deflator worth remembering: an "n₀ exists" theorem proved through the regularity lemma converts an open problem into a DECIDABLE one on paper while making it strictly less attackable in practice.

entries.upstream_handle: FALSIFIABLE ("Open, but could be disproved with a finite counterexample"). Not formalised — erdosproblems.com/743 reports "Formalised statement? No".
entries.statement_short: Gyárfás tree packing conjecture: for any trees T_2,...,T_n with T_k having exactly k vertices, K_n is the edge-disjoint union of the T_k.
entries.what_a_witness_is: A counterexample witness is a specific tuple of 9 unlabeled trees (T_2,...,T_10), each given as a parent array / edge list, that admits no edge-disjoint packing into K_10 — accompanied by an exhaustive refutation (search tree). A positive witness (per tuple) is the packing itself: an assignment of each tree's edges to distinct edges of K_10. Note the edge count is exact: sum_{k=2}^{10}(k−1) = 45 = C(10,2), so this is a perfect decomposition, not a packing with slack.
entries.smallest_untested_case: n = 10. Fishburn [Fi83] settled n ≤ 9. The n=10 instance is the 45,376,056 tuples (T_2,...,T_10) of unlabeled trees.
entries.known_computational_frontier: Fishburn, "Packing graphs with odd and even trees", J. Graph Theory 7 (1983) 369–383 — verified n ≤ 9. This is still the frontier cited on erdosproblems.com/743 (page curated 2026). Structural partial results reduce the work but do not settle n=10: Gyárfás–Lehel [GyLe78] (all but ≤2 trees stars, or all stars/paths); Bollobás [Bo83] (the smallest ⌊n/√2⌋ trees pack greedily — for n=10 that is T_2..T_8, leaving only T_9,T_10 and 17 edges); Joos–Kim–Kühn–Osthus [JKKO19] (bounded max degree); Janzer–Montgomery [JaMo24] (largest cn trees). A claimed full proof exists — Chalise, Clark & Gnang, arXiv:2410.13840v2 (23 Oct 2024) — but it is disputed: on the #743 forum thread Zach Hunter (01 Mar 2026) reports that people who tried to verify it "did not have faith in the present arguments", the site still lists the problem OPEN with 0 accepted claimed proofs, and there is no refereed version.
entries.search_space_estimate: Unlabeled trees on k vertices (A000055) for k=2..10: 1,1,2,3,6,11,23,47,106 → 1·1·2·3·6·11·23·47·106 = 45,376,056 tuples. Per tuple, T_10 is spanning so its embedding is free up to relabeling K_10; the residual DFS over embeddings of T_9,...,T_2 into the remaining 36 edges is ~10^4–10^6 nodes worst case and terminates on first success for the (believed overwhelming) majority. Total ≈ 4.5×10^7 × 10^4–10^5 ≈ 10^11–10^12 primitive ops — one workstation, days. Next case n=11 multiplies by A000055(11)=235 → 1.07×10^10 tuples, which is the wall.
entries.verdict_reason: All four criteria hold. (1) A witness is 9 small trees plus an edge assignment — pure integer data. (2) 4.5×10^7 tuples with a ~10^11–10^12 total op budget sits inside the one-workstation line, and Bollobás's greedy result shrinks the hard part of each tuple to placing just T_9 and T_10 into 17 remaining edges. (3) Verifying a packing is checking that 45 edges are used exactly once and that 9 subgraphs are isomorphic to the prescribed trees — trivial, exact, dependency-free, no floats. (4) The frontier has stood at n ≤ 9 since Fishburn 1983 (43 years) with no evidence anyone extended it; the one claim of a general proof is unrefereed and community-doubted, which if anything raises the value of an independent finite check at n=10. Payoff is asymmetric and good: almost certainly every tuple packs, yielding "tree packing conjecture verified for n=10, first extension since 1983" as a clean replayable record; and if a tuple resists, we have the first counterexample candidate. CAVEAT to price in: the deliverable certificate is 45M packings, so ship the search program + hashes + a replay harness rather than a monolithic artifact, and be explicit that a NEGATIVE tuple needs an exhaustive-refutation certificate, which is the expensive side.

entries.upstream_handle: https://www.erdosproblems.com/779 (FALSIFIABLE; Deaconescu, via Guy [Gu83]; OEIS A005235)
entries.statement_short: For n > 1 let P = p_1···p_n be the n-th primorial. Must there always exist a prime p with p_n < p < P such that P + p is prime?
entries.what_a_witness_is: NOT concrete in any usable sense. A counterexample is an index n together with a proof that P + p is composite for EVERY prime p in (p_n, P) — i.e. π(P) ≈ P/ln P compositeness certificates on numbers of size P. There is no small object to exhibit.
entries.smallest_untested_case: n = 2001. (The site cites Deaconescu for n ≤ 1000; OEIS A005235 does better — see frontier.)
entries.known_computational_frontier: Site remark: Deaconescu verified n ≤ 1000. Stronger, and apparently not noted on the problem page: OEIS A005235 (Fortunate numbers a(n) = least m > 1 with p_n# + m prime) records that the first 2000 terms are prime (J. Arndt, Apr 2013), and Firoozbakht's observation a(n) > p_{n+1} − 1 means each such a(n) is a prime p with p_n < p < P and P + p prime. So #779 is in fact verified for all n ≤ 2000. Batalov's b-file extends A005235 to n = 4600, though primality of every one of those terms is not asserted.
entries.search_space_estimate: Certifying a counterexample at n = 2001: P = p_2000# with log P ≈ θ(17389) ≈ 17389, so P ≈ e^17389 (~7550 decimal digits) and π(P) ≈ P/ln P ≈ 10^7548 primality tests on 7550-digit numbers. That is 10^7536 times over any conceivable budget.
entries.verdict_reason: Fails criterion 3 catastrophically and criterion 1 outright. 'Falsifiable' here is a technicality: the counterexample is an n, but *checking* that n is a counterexample is an exhaustion over ~10^7548 huge primality tests. Nothing is exhibitable. The heuristic in the site's own remark puts the failure probability at ≈exp(−n^{cn}) — Cambie's phrasing is that the chances of failing are ridiculously small — so we would be paying an astronomical price to hunt an object that essentially certainly does not exist. The only tractable work here is extending the *verification* side (Fortunate-number primality), which is a records-ladder increment, not a resolution, and OEIS already sits at n ≤ 2000 for free.

entries.upstream_handle: VERIFIABLE (open, but could be proved with a finite example)
entries.statement_short: Is there k>2 such that the k-subsets of {1,...,2k} can be coloured with k+1 colours so that every (k+1)-subset sees all k+1 colours among its k-subsets? Equivalently: is chi(J(2k,k)) = k+1 for some k>2, where J(2k,k) is the Johnson graph (k-sets adjacent iff they meet in k-1 elements)? Erdos-Rosenfeld [Er74d, p.283]; k+1 <= chi(J(2k,k)) <= 2k always.
entries.what_a_witness_is: CONCRETE. An explicit proper (k+1)-colouring of J(2k,k): a map from the C(2k,k) k-subsets of [2k] into {1,...,k+1} with no two sets meeting in exactly k-1 elements getting the same colour. Equivalently a partition of all k-subsets into k+1 constant-weight codes of length 2k, weight k, minimum Hamming distance 4. Storable as C(2k,k) bytes (184,756 bytes at k=10).
entries.smallest_untested_case: k = 10, i.e. decide whether chi(J(20,10)) = 11. Ma-Tang Thm 2.2 kills every k>2 with k+1 composite, so the only live k are k = p-1 for odd prime p: {4, 6, 10, 12, 16, 18, 22, ...}. Brouwer's table already kills k=4 (chi(J(8,4))=6>5) and k=6 (chi(J(12,6)) in [8,9] > 7). k=10 is the first survivor.
entries.known_computational_frontier: Brouwer's Johnson-graph chromatic-number table (https://www.win.tue.nl/~aeb/graphs/Johnson.html, built on Brouwer-Shearer-Sloane-Smith 1990, Etzion-Bitan 1996, Brouwer-Etzion 2011) gives values/bounds only up to n=16: chi(J(6,3))=6, chi(J(8,4))=6, chi(J(10,5))=8, chi(J(12,6)) in [8,9], chi(J(14,7)) in [10,14], chi(J(16,8)) in [10,15] -- all strictly above k+1, so k=3..8 are dead (this is what settles the k=6 case Erdos and Rosenfeld were unsure about). Jie Ma and Quanyu Tang, 'A note on Erdos problem #835' (Oct 2025, github.com/QuanyuTang/erdos-problem-835): if k>2 and k+1 is not prime then chi(J(2k,k)) >= k+2; their Lemma 2.3 proves their divisibility method provably CANNOT touch k+1 prime. Nothing computed at n=20.
entries.search_space_estimate: C(20,10) = 184,756 vertices, degree 10*10 = 100, edges = 184756*100/2 = 9,237,800; an 11-colouring SAT instance is 184,756*11 = 2,032,316 booleans and 9,237,800*11 = 101,615,800 edge clauses (naive space 11^184756).
entries.verdict_reason: Criteria 1 and 3 pass cleanly (the object is a byte array; checking it is 2*9,237,800 = 1.85e7 integer comparisons, no floats), but 2 and 4 fail. The VERIFIABLE handle only fires in the direction of EXISTENCE, and every data point says no such k exists: chi(J(2k,k)) already runs 2-3 above k+1 by k=7,8, and Ma-Tang shows the only survivors are a thin prime-indexed subsequence they could not reach. So a witness hunt is a hunt for an object nobody believes is there. Settling the smallest live case k=10 the other way (chi(J(20,10)) > 11) is a 2.03M-variable / 101.6M-clause UNSAT with a 20!-sized automorphism group -- not a one-workstation job, and a symmetry-prescribed search that comes back empty proves nothing. Adjacent honest work exists (the open cells of Brouwer's table, e.g. chi(J(10,4)) in [8,9], chi(J(12,4)) in [10,11]) but that is a different, non-Erdos frontier.

entries.upstream_handle: https://www.erdosproblems.com/848 (DECIDABLE; Erdős–Sárközy [Er92b,p.239])
entries.statement_short: Is the maximum size of A ⊆ {1,…,N} with ab+1 never squarefree (all a,b ∈ A) achieved by taking n ≡ 7 (mod 25)?
entries.what_a_witness_is: Two-sided and asymmetric. A falsifying witness is a set A ⊆ {1..N} with |A| > ⌈(N−7)/25⌉ and ab+1 non-squarefree for every pair — cheap and exact to verify by squarefree-sieving ab+1 ≤ N²+1. But closing the DECIDABLE gap requires the other side: an exact maximum-clique certificate for every N in the remaining interval, on the graph with vertices {a ≤ N : a²+1 not squarefree} (density ≈0.105N) and edges ab+1 not squarefree. That is NP-hard per N.
entries.smallest_untested_case: N ≈ 10^3 upward. Alexeev reports straightforward approaches only reached 'a few hundred'; MalekZ's claimed structured verification to N = 10^7 was reviewed and judged likely incorrect (N. Sothanaphan, 16 Mar 2026) so it cannot be counted. The interval to close runs up to N_0 ≈ 2.64×10^17.
entries.known_computational_frontier: Sawhney's note settles the problem for all sufficiently large N, originally at the ineffective-in-practice N_0 = exp(1420) ≈ 10^617. A GPT-5.4-Thinking-driven explicit-threshold campaign on the #848 thread (N. Sothanaphan, Mar 2026) walked N_0 down 7×10^17 → 3.3×10^17 → 2.64×10^17, with cross-model pingpong (old-bielefelder) suggesting ~2.9×10^17 is roughly the structural floor of that proof method. Upper bound |A| ≤ (0.108…+o(1))N (van Doorn), sharpened to ≈0.105 (Weisenberg).
entries.search_space_estimate: Closing the finite check means deciding the exact maximum clique for every N in (10^3, 2.64×10^17] — 2.6×10^17 instances, each NP-hard on ≈0.105N vertices. Even at one operation per N that is 2.6×10^17 ops, five orders of magnitude over budget before any per-instance cost is counted; MalekZ's (unsound) run to only 10^7 already cost ~a day of compute.
entries.verdict_reason: This is the classic 'decidable up to a finite check' trap and it should be recorded as one. The tag is honest — Sawhney closed large N and the threshold is now explicit — but the residual interval is 2.6×10^17 wide and each point in it is an NP-hard exact max-clique, so the finite check cannot be completed by compute at any scale we or anyone else has. The two ends are also moving toward each other on the wrong side: the theory end has already been squeezed to within ~10% of its structural floor by a multi-model campaign, and the computational end is stuck around 10^3–10^7 with the one claimed 10^7 result judged likely wrong. The falsification side (a set beating 7 mod 25) IS cheaply verifiable, but Sawhney's structure theorem says no such set exists once |A| ≥ (1/25−c)N and N is large, and small-N brute force is already done — so there is no window where a witness hunt is both cheap and unexplored. Progress here needs a better explicit threshold, i.e. analytic number theory, not a farm.

entries.upstream_handle: FALSIFIABLE — "Open, but could be disproved with a finite counterexample" (erdosproblems.com/982, last edited 19 Oct 2025)
entries.statement_short: If n distinct points in R^2 form a convex polygon, some vertex has at least floor(n/2) different distances to the other vertices. Regular n-gon shows floor(n/2) is best possible. Formalised in FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/982.lean (research open, AMS 52).
entries.what_a_witness_is: Concrete: n points in R^2 in convex position such that EVERY vertex sees at most floor(n/2)-1 distinct distances to the other n-1 vertices. Real coordinates — the object is a point configuration, not a combinatorial structure.
entries.smallest_untested_case: n = 8: need a convex octagon in which every vertex has at most 3 distinct distances (floor(8/2)=4). n<=7 is forced by the proved lower bounds: Erdos-Fishburn f(n) >= floor(n/3+1) gives 3 at n=7 = floor(7/2), and gives only 3 at n=8 < 4. I verified numerically that Harborth's H_8 (unit square + equilateral triangles erected on each side), the known 8-point set with exactly 3 distinct distances from every point, has a convex hull of only 4 vertices — so it does NOT settle n=8, which is consistent with the problem still being open.
entries.known_computational_frontier: No exhaustive small-n computation found in the literature. The frontier is analytic: Moser [Mo52] f(n) >= ceil(n/3); Erdos-Fishburn [ErFi94] f(n) >= floor(n/3+1); Dumitrescu [Du06b] f(n) >= ceil((13n-6)/36); best known Nivasch-Pach-Pinchasi-Zerbib, J. Comput. Geom. 4 (2013) 1-12: f(n) >= (13/36 + 1/22701)n - O(1) ~= 0.36112n. Altman proved the weaker total-count statement (n points in convex position determine >= floor(n/2) distances); the per-vertex form is what remains open. Related few-distance-set classification: Erdos-Fishburn (Discrete Math 160 (1996) 115-125) for k<=4, Shinohara (Discrete Math 308 (2008) 3048-3055) for k=5, Wei (EJC 19 (2012) #P38) for k=6.
entries.search_space_estimate: Continuum: 8 points x 2 coords = 16 reals, minus 4 similarity d.o.f. = a 12-dimensional real semialgebraic feasibility problem; the discrete shell is at most 3^C(8,2) = 3^28 ~= 2.3e13 per-vertex distance-class labelings, and EACH leaf then needs a real-solvability (Groebner/CAD) decision in 12 unknowns — not 1e13 primitive ops but 1e13 CAD calls.
entries.verdict_reason: Fails criteria 2 and 3. The witness is concrete (criterion 1 passes) but the search space is a 12-dimensional continuum, not a finite set: the enumerable part is only the distance-equality pattern, and every pattern leaf is a real-quantifier-elimination problem. Verification is exact only if the counterexample happens to have rational coordinates, and every known extremal few-distance configuration (regular polygons, H_8, eigensolver's 21-gon pair with r a root of x^3-x^2-2x+1) is irrational-algebraic — confirming such a witness needs a CAS, which is precisely what we exclude. The theoretical gap 0.361n vs 0.5n has resisted four successive papers over 60 years with the last improvement (1/22701) being cosmetic, which is the signature of a hard analytic obstruction, not a missed search.

entries.upstream_handle: FALSIFIABLE (open, but could be disproved with a finite counterexample)
entries.statement_short: The independent-set sequence of any tree or forest is unimodal: if i_k(G) counts independent vertex sets of size k, then for every forest T there is m with i_0(T) <= ... <= i_m(T) >= i_{m+1}(T) >= ... . Alavi-Malde-Schwenk-Erdos 1987 [AMSE87], who showed it is false for general graphs (every inequality pattern is realised).
entries.what_a_witness_is: CONCRETE and tiny. A single tree T on n vertices whose independence sequence is not unimodal -- storable as an (n-1)-entry parent array (about 30 bytes). No auxiliary data required.
entries.smallest_untested_case: n = 30 (all trees on at most 29 vertices have been exhaustively verified). n=31 and n=32 are the next rungs.
entries.known_computational_frontier: Exhaustive verification for all trees on at most 29 vertices: B. Reynolds, 'Mean bounds, structural reductions, and exhaustive verification for tree independence polynomial unimodality', Zenodo preprint v3, March 2026, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19100781 -- cited as the state of the art ('As of April 2026 ... computationally verified for trees on at most 29 vertices') in Hibi-Kara-Vien, arXiv:2604.18824, 20 Apr 2026. Earlier rungs: Yosef-Mizrachi-Kadrawi arXiv:2101.06744 verified n<=20 (via log-concavity); Kadrawi-Levit arXiv:2305.01784 found exactly two trees on 26 vertices that break LOG-CONCAVITY, which implies an exhaustive n=26 enumeration; Ramos-Sun arXiv:2510.18826 ran PatternBoost (Charton-Ellenberg-Wagner-Williamson) over trees of 27-101 vertices and found tens of thousands of log-concavity counterexamples but NO unimodality counterexample. Caveat: the n<=29 frontier rests on an unrefereed Zenodo preprint.
entries.search_space_estimate: A000055(30) = 14,830,871,802 unlabeled trees; each costs an O(n*alpha) integer DP with i_k < 2^30 (fits uint64), about 1e3 word ops, so ~1.5e13 primitive ops -- hours on one 16-core box with nauty gentreeg (~1e6-1e7 trees/s/core). n=31 = 4.03e10 trees (~1 day), n=32 = 1.10e11 (~days).
entries.verdict_reason: The only one of the five that clears all four bars. The witness is a 30-byte parent array; the check is a dependency-free exact integer DP with no float and no CAS; the smallest untested size n=30 costs ~1.5e13 ops, inside the ~1e12-with-pruning budget once the published structural reductions are applied and comfortably inside one workstation-day even brute force; and the frontier is a specific published number (29) rather than a vague 'small cases'. Two honest caveats, neither fatal: (a) the payoff is asymmetric -- Ramos-Sun's ML sweep to 101 vertices found no unimodality break, so the realistic deliverable is a 'verified to n=30/31' record for the Records lane, not a solved Erdos problem; (b) the n<=29 claim is an unrefereed Zenodo preprint, which makes independently reproducing n<=29 a genuine first-step contribution rather than wasted motion, and gives a built-in correctness gate before we spend anything on n=30. Recommend building the verifier against the known n<=20 and n=26 results (which must reproduce the two known log-concavity breaks) before extending.

entries.upstream_handle: FALSIFIABLE (open, but could be disproved with a finite counterexample)
entries.statement_short: Erdos matching conjecture [Er65d]: for f(n;r,k) = max edges in an r-uniform hypergraph on n vertices with no k pairwise disjoint edges, f(n;r,k) = max(C(rk-1,r), C(n,r)-C(n-k+1,r)) for all r >= 3. Both terms are achieved by explicit constructions; Erdos-Gallai proved r=2.
entries.what_a_witness_is: CONCRETE. An r-uniform hypergraph H on n vertices (a list of r-subsets) with no k pairwise disjoint edges and strictly more edges than the conjectured maximum. At the smallest live cell that is a subset of the 715 4-subsets of [13].
entries.smallest_untested_case: r=4, k=3, n=13 -- the smallest cell not covered by ANY range listed on the problem page (small-n side: trivial for n<kr=12, Kleitman at n=12, Frankl [Fr17] reaches only n <= 3*(4 + 1/(2*4^9)) = 12.0000006; large-n side: the best listed for r=4 is Frankl-Luczak-Mieczkowska n > 2k*r^2/log r = 69.3, i.e. n >= 70). So the listed gap for (r,k)=(4,3) is 13 <= n <= 69. The genuinely hard regime, however, is n ~ (r+1)k with k -> infinity, where nothing is finite.
entries.known_computational_frontier: No exhaustive computation of f(n;r,k) is cited anywhere on the problem page; every listed advance (Kleitman 1968, Frankl 1987/2017, Frankl-Furedi, Bollobas-Daykin-Erdos 1976, Frankl-Rodl-Rucinski 2012, Huang-Loh-Sudakov 2012, Frankl-Luczak-Mieczkowska 2012, Luczak-Mieczkowska 2014, Kolupaev-Kupavskii 2023) is a THEOREM covering an infinite range, not a search. r=3 is fully settled. Very recent unvetted preprints attack r=4 with heavy machinery: arXiv:2605.26060 (May 2026, finite-board reduction, claims 4-uniform for all s >= 6961 via exact Farkas/branch-and-bound certificates on a 19-vertex board) and arXiv:2607.07392 (July 2026, claimed spectral confirmation). Neither is vetted; both signal the cell we could compute is not where the problem lives.
entries.search_space_estimate: At r=4,k=3,n=13: C(13,4)=715 candidate edges, so 2^715 families; as an ILP, 715 binaries with 715*C(9,4)*C(5,4)/3! = 75,075 no-3-matching constraints -- trivially small, and the conjectured optimum is max(330, 385) = 385. At r=4,k=4,n=17: 2,380 binaries, 44,669,625 constraints. But the conjecture's hard range is n ~ (r+1)k as k grows, where the space is 2^C(n,r) with no bound at all.
entries.verdict_reason: Inverted feasibility: the cells small enough for us to decide exactly are the cells theory already owns, and the cells theory does not own are unbounded. r=4,k=3,n=13 is a 715-variable ILP we could finish in minutes -- but a counterexample there would contradict a 60-year consensus and several published theorems abutting it, and finding none reproduces nothing publishable. Push k up to reach genuinely untouched territory and the constraint count explodes (4.5e7 already at k=4,n=17) while an S_n symmetry group makes proving ILP optimality, not just feasibility, the real cost. The FALSIFIABLE tag is technically true and operationally empty: the witness, if it exists at all, lives at large k where the search space is 2^C(n,r) with no finite ceiling. Two independent teams are currently claiming r=4 by theory, not by search; we have no edge.

entries.upstream_handle: FALSIFIABLE — "Open, but could be disproved with a finite counterexample" (erdosproblems.com/1041, last edited 06 Dec 2025)
entries.statement_short: For f(z) = prod (z - z_i) with all |z_i| < 1, must there always exist a path of length less than 2 inside {z : |f(z)| < 1} connecting two of the roots? EHP58 proved the weaker component lemma (some component of the sublevel set contains >= 2 roots). Formalised in FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/1041.lean.
entries.what_a_witness_is: NOT concrete in the operational sense. A witness is a set of n roots in the open unit disk together with a PROOF that no path of length < 2 inside {|f|<1} joins any two roots. The roots are a finite object; the certifying property is an infimum over an infinite-dimensional space of paths in a semialgebraic region.
entries.smallest_untested_case: Degree n = 5. Pendyala proved the degree-four case (arXiv:2606.24875, 23 Jun 2026) and reports it formalised and verified in Lean 4.22; degrees 1-3 are trivial/known. So a counterexample must have at least 5 roots.
entries.known_computational_frontier: No numerical or exhaustive search reported. Direction of evidence is strongly TOWARD the conjecture being true: degree 4 is proved and Lean-checked; a full claimed proof (shtuka, Mar 2026, gradient-flow-tree strategy) received a detailed review from Terence Tao who initially rated it plausibly correct, then found and demonstrated a fatal topological gap in Proposition 12 by plotting the flow lines of z^2-1 — his conclusion was that the flow does not organise into trees at all and the whole area-integral strategy cannot isolate the right geometry. A separate GPT-5.4 claimed solution (Apr 2026) was killed by a decisive gap in its Lemma 6. Tao and Sothanaphan also considered the counterexample direction via Mac Lane's winding lemniscates [problem 1215] and noted explicitly that Mac Lane's argument controls paths but does NOT control roots, so it does not yield a construction. Adjacent: Pendyala arXiv:2606.19178 proves c*sqrt(log n) <= S(n) <= pi*n — but S(n) is a DIFFERENT quantity (shortest path from 0 to the unit circle inside {|z|<=1, |f|<=1}), not root-to-root, so it does not refute this problem.
entries.search_space_estimate: Continuum with no finite shell: degree 5 gives 5 roots x 2 coords = 10 reals, minus rotation = a 9-dimensional continuum, and unlike the distance problems there is no discrete combinatorial surrogate to enumerate, because the falsifying property is metric (a geodesic length lower bound), not combinatorial. UNKNOWN as an operation count — it is not a finite search.
entries.verdict_reason: The worst of the four and the clearest WALL. Fails criterion 1: the finite object (5 complex numbers) does not carry its own certificate — certifying it requires a global lower bound on the geodesic distance between roots inside a semialgebraic sublevel set, i.e. proving a non-existence over an infinite-dimensional path space. Fails criterion 3 absolutely: there is no cheap exact check; the candidate-verification problem is itself a research-grade continuous-optimisation/topology problem. Fails criterion 4 by direction: two independent expert-reviewed attempts are pushing toward a POSITIVE proof, degree 4 is already closed, and the only known source of pathological lemniscate geometry (Mac Lane) was examined by Tao and Sothanaphan and explicitly found not to control root placement. Hunting a witness here is betting against the visible gradient of the field. The upstream FALSIFIABLE tag is nominal, not operational.

entries.upstream_handle: FALSIFIABLE — "Open, but could be disproved with a finite counterexample" (erdosproblems.com/1082, last edited 11 Apr 2026)
entries.statement_short: Let A be n points in R^2 with no three on a line. Does A determine at least floor(n/2) distinct distances? (Part i, OPEN — a conjecture of Szemeredi, who proved it with n/3.) Part ii, the stronger per-point form, is ALREADY REFUTED and is marked `research solved` in the Lean file.
entries.what_a_witness_is: Concrete: n points in R^2, no three collinear, whose total distinct-distance count is at most floor(n/2)-1. Equivalently a planar k-distance set of size n >= 2k+2 with no three points collinear. Real coordinates.
entries.smallest_untested_case: n = 16 with 7 distances. The ladder: a counterexample needs a k-distance set of size >= 2k+2, and the maximum size g(k) of a planar k-distance set is known for k<=6 — g(1..6) = 3,5,7,9,12,13. k=5 needs n=12 and g(5)=12 exactly, but Shinohara proved the maximum planar 5-distance set is UNIQUE and it is a triangular-lattice piece, which has collinear triples, so n=12 is closed. k=6 needs n=14 > g(6)=13, closed. g(7) is unknown, so the first genuinely open slot is n=16 with 7 distances. (Note: part ii's counterexamples — Harborth's H_8 with 3 distances per point, and eigensolver's 42-point double-21-gon with 20 per point — do NOT touch part i, because their TOTAL distinct-distance counts are large.)
entries.known_computational_frontier: Szemeredi's n/3 (unpublished, given in [Er75f]) is still the record lower bound. Few-distance-set classification: Erdos-Fishburn, Discrete Math 160 (1996) 115-125 (k<=4); Shinohara, Discrete Math 308 (2008) 3048-3055 (uniqueness of the maximum 5-distance set, 12 points); Wei Xianglin, EJC 19 (2012) #P38 (g(6)=13). Directed searches on the problem itself: StijnC checked all odd n <= 250 in the concentric-regular-n-gon family (forum, 16 Oct 2025) — but under a restricted equal-distance condition, and eigensolver found the n=42 example his sweep missed. A DeepMind prover agent ran autonomously on the Lean statement (Feb 2026) and rediscovered Harborth's H_8; Sharvil Kesarwani then traced it to Fishburn's 2002 paper. This space has already been swept by an automated searcher.
entries.search_space_estimate: Continuum: 16 points x 2 coords - 4 similarity d.o.f. = 28 free reals; the discrete shell is at most 7^C(16,2) = 7^120 ~= 1e101 distance-class labelings, each needing a real-solvability decision in 28 unknowns. Roughly 90 orders of magnitude past a workstation.
entries.verdict_reason: Fails criteria 2, 3 and 4. (2) 1e101 labelings over a 28-dimensional continuum. (3) The two witnesses actually produced for the (easier, now-solved) part ii both required a CAS or an ITP to confirm — eigensolver flagged his own precision errors and asked for help, StijnC verified with Maple, llllvvuu verified in Lean via Aristotle. The critical radius is a root of x^3-x^2-2x+1; exact integer squared-distance checking is not available. (4) A DeepMind autonomous prover already swept this problem and produced only a construction that turned out to be 24 years old in the literature. The remaining part i is genuinely harder than the part that AI search cracked, and the obstruction is that the known extremal few-distance sets all live in the triangular lattice, which the no-3-collinear hypothesis forbids by construction.
